Content.ParaText: It is my duty to lay before the House, pursuant to subsection 7(3) of the Auditor General Act, the 2026 reports of the Auditor General of Canada.
Pursuant to Standing Order 108(3)(g), these documents are deemed permanently referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Judy A. Sgro (Humber River—Black Creek, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the fourth report of the Liaison Committee, entitled “Committee Activities and Expenditures April 1-August 31, 2026”.
Mr. Speaker, this petition is timely in that people from Disability Without Poverty are here on Parliament Hill.

The petitioners are calling on the federal government to stop the duplication of making people prove they are living with a disability after they have already been deemed living with a disability in their province or territory. They want the Government of Canada to accept provincial and territorial disability determinations as sufficient evidence of eligibility for the disability tax credit when equivalent eligibility criteria have not been met; amend the Income Tax Act and related regulations to eliminate unnecessary duplicative medical certification requirements for the disability tax credit; ensure that eligible Canadians can access the disability tax credit and the Canada disability benefit without unnecessary barriers or delays; and work with the provinces, the territories, disability organizations and health care professionals to create a streamlined disability eligibility process that reduces red tape, improves access to supports and allows family physicians to spend more time caring for patients rather than completing duplicative government paperwork.
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to table a petition signed by the people of Moonbeam, Ontario.

Communities across northern Ontario are calling on this government to recognize Trans-Canada Highway 11 as a project of national interest. Every day of inaction is another day where lives are at risk on this highway, which was closed again just last week.

Moonbeam will certainly not be the last community to sign this petition. We are going door to door and village to village, and the message is the same everywhere. Northern Ontario is asking for action.
Designate Trans-Canada Highway 11 as a project of national interest.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Alleged Premature Disclosure of Bill C-40—Speaker's Ruling

Content.ParaText: I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on October 6, 2026, by the House leader of the official opposition concerning the alleged premature disclosure of Bill C-40, an act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security.

During his intervention, the House leader of the official opposition argued that specific details of Bill C-40 had been shared with journalists before the bill was introduced in the House. He based his assertion on two news articles published before the bill was introduced in the House, which, in his opinion, provided substantive information that could not have been gleaned from the title of the bill, nor deduced from previous government consultations and announcements. The member noted that these articles cited anonymous sources who were not authorized to discuss this information publicly. He posited that such a disclosure constituted a contempt of the House.

For his part, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House asserted that there is no prima facie question of privilege. He assured the House that, following its own investigation, the government found no evidence that anyone leaked the contents of the bill while it was on notice. The parliamentary secretary also argued that the legislative details discussed in the news articles in question have been in the public domain as matters of government policy for some time, speaking specifically to deliberations and consultations undertaken by the government on defence procurement and other topics related to the bill. He assured the House that these conversations did not occur at a time even close to the notice of the bill. Finally, he suggested that the information cited in the news articles was at times speculative and uncertain, casting further doubt on the possibility that specific provisions of the bill were divulged.

During a second intervention, the House leader of the official opposition sought to rebut some of the parliamentary secretary's arguments. He questioned the scope and thoroughness of the government's investigation before it concluded that no internal leak had occurred. He also argued that the policy information the government claimed was already in the public domain could not account for everything revealed in the news articles.

Members are right to affirm that it is a long-standing expectation that the House must be the first to be informed of the details of specific legislative measures that will come before it. As explained by Speaker Milliken in his ruling of March 19, 2001, on page 1840 of the Debates:

Quote.QuotePara: The convention of the confidentiality of bills on notice is necessary, not only so that members themselves may be well informed, but also because of the pre-eminent [role] which the House plays and must play in the legislative affairs of the nation.

Content.ParaText: The Chair has on many occasions been asked to rule on matters regarding the right of the House to have first access to legislative measures, including recently in the current session. One factor to consider is whether the allegation has been met with any admission or denial of responsibility, or alternative explanations. In the case before us, the Chair is faced with two different assertions, one claiming that the rights of the House were violated, and another, from the government, denying that details of one of its bills were prematurely divulged. In other words, the facts are disputed. This is reminiscent of other situations where, taking members at their word, the Chair was reluctant to intervene.
However, it is important to note that the government's responsibility is not the only element that must be considered by the Chair. Speaker Rota stated on March 9, 2021, at page 4762 of the Debates:

Quote.QuotePara: While there is indeed a well-established practice that a member must be taken at their word, the fact remains that the government's stating that it is not responsible for the premature disclosure of a bill is not in itself sufficient to convince the Chair. I would add that the source of information is one factor among others and that it is important first and foremost to determine whether precise details were provided before the House was made aware of them. The Chair must thus take into consideration all the information before it and reach a conclusion based on the facts presented by the members.

Content.ParaText: With this in mind, I felt it appropriate to review the news articles in question and the text of Bill C-40 now before the House. Having done so, I find that the similarities between the text of the bill and the details in the news articles remain at a high level and do not provide sufficient grounds to conclude that a leak of the bill itself has occurred. Further to this point, while members may be correct in stating that the details published in the news articles go beyond what is revealed in the bill's long title, this cannot stand as a reliable test for judging whether the precise contents of a bill have been divulged.

The Chair also notes that the news articles do not directly address the question of whether the sources cited had access to a copy of the bill itself, or to its specific provisions, and were therefore even in a position to share it, nor has any convincing evidence been brought to the Chair's attention that would demonstrate that the sharing of information between the sources and journalists, or between the government and the sources, took place in the window between when the bill was placed on notice and when the bill was introduced.

During his intervention, the parliamentary secretary stated that related public consultations were taking place well before Bill C-40 was placed on notice. As Speaker Regan affirmed in his ruling of June 8, 2017, at page 12320 of the Debates:

Quote.QuotePara: The right of the House to first access to legislation is one of our oldest conventions. It does and must, however, coexist with the need of governments to consult widely, with the public and stakeholders alike, on issues and policies in the preparation of legislation.

Content.ParaText: After reviewing all the evidence provided, the Chair cannot determine with any degree of certainty that the entirety of the bill, or specific sections thereof, were divulged prior to its introduction in the House. The government's assurance that it has no knowledge of a leak, the substance of the details published in the news articles and the lack of clarity around the nature and timing of the anonymous sources' information all contribute to this conclusion. Accordingly, the Chair does not find that this case constitutes a prima facie question of privilege.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed from October 28 consideration of the motion that Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Yasir Naqvi (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of International Trade and to the Secretary of State (International Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is a great honour for me to stand to speak to Bill C-34, the safe social media act.

In my capacity as the very proud member of Parliament for Ottawa Centre, this issue is extremely important and personal to me as a parent. I have a 14-year-old son and a 10-year-old daughter, so I am in the thick and thin of social media and smart devices like cellphones and iPads, making sure that I am continuously engaged with my children when it comes to issues around the safe use of social media. Probably one of the biggest issues that I hear from my constituents on a regular basis, especially those who are parents or grandparents, is how to ensure that we have safe access to social media. I am sure members will agree with me that AI comes up in pretty much every single conversation nowadays. People want to ensure that there are strong regulations to monitor all these things.

As a result of the many conversations I had with my constituents over several months, and I am sure all of us know of the barbecues and different events that take place, I took the liberty of sending a mailer to my constituents, a questionnaire specifically on Bill C-34, the safe social media act, asking them some really important questions so they could help guide me, and hopefully all of us, on how best to navigate this important issue and on the important features that my constituents would like to see in the legislation.

What I asked in this questionnaire, which I sent to all the residents in my riding of Ottawa Centre, were questions like, “How should the government prioritize keeping young Canadians safe online?” and “As the government implements the legislation, what should it prioritize and how?” I also asked my constituents the question, “Which online harms concern you most for the young people in your lives?” We also asked for their experience in online safety and, more specifically, questions concerning the proposed age restriction for social media accounts, which is suggested in the legislation to be 16 plus.

First of all, I want to thank all my constituents for so enthusiastically writing on this issue. Not only did they send the mailer back after filling out the questions, but they went online, because we had a Google Forms questionnaire available, and participated. They have approached me on the streets and at community events to talk about this as well.

I think a few things really came out of that. There is, as I mentioned earlier, a strong concern as to the safe use of social media. People really want government to step forward and bring in regulations, controls and monitoring so that social media is safe, especially for children, but for seniors as well. I got a very strong sense that there is support for legislation like Bill C-34 from my constituents of Ottawa Centre. One of the key reasons is that people want to protect our children and want legislation. They want Parliament and the government to take steps in that regard.

There is also support for a restriction on the use of social media until age 16. I got a very good sense, from the survey results we got back and from my conversations, that people want to make sure there is some sort of age limitation on who can use social media, and 16 seems to be the right age. I will say that if we talk to young people, there is push-back on that, including from my 14-year-old, who understands the benefits and harms around social media but has probed me as to why the age is 16. I think the most important issue that has come up in my conversations is how we are going to regulate that.

It is one thing to say we will restrict the use of or access to social media to 16-year-olds. The question then becomes how we are going to enforce that rule. There is an understanding that young people being young people, they will find ways to get around it. Of course, everybody is looking at places such as Australia in that regard. I think an important element that, as legislators, we should be focused on throughout this legislation is how best to enforce the rule, because people want a rule like that in place but also want to ensure that it is not just a rule on paper. They want effective implementation and enforcement of the rule as well.

That is why I personally like the idea that we would not just be putting a blanket ban, so to speak, in the legislation. There would be a provision that, if certain standards are met to ensure that there is safe social media, those platforms may be allowed to operate. I think there is a better path, compared to the one in jurisdictions such as Australia, embedded in this legislation, which would allow for access to social media as long as certain standards are met that would ensure that the information our kids have access to is safe.

The second point I want to raise, which is something I said at the outset, is that there is a huge concern around AI and its content, the nature of information that is available. Misinformation and disinformation continue to come up in the conversation, and we saw that in the survey documents we received. There is a very significant concern about misleading information that is AI-manipulated and about content that has been altered through AI.

I think it would be an understatement if I said that deepfake images and videos are a serious concern that people are grappling with. I heard about this through the consultation process I did in my community. People want assurances that we are taking the necessary steps to make sure that deepfake images and videos are regulated, are monitored and are not allowed, because there are some serious concerns.

There are serious concerns from seniors in this regard. I know that much of the focus of the bill is toward young people and teenagers, but there are some serious concerns in our communities on the part of seniors as well who are being exposed to information that looks awfully close to being real. They are concerned about whether information is accurate or not and whether they have been taken advantage of. There are scams being developed. We know that our seniors are quite vulnerable to those kind of scams, frauds, phishing expeditions, etc. There is a real concern from the elderly constituents in my riding of Ottawa Centre on this issue.

I think the legislation has a lot of important elements. I am supportive of the legislation and would ask my colleagues of the House to support it as well. I think it would address a very important issue. We know that social media has become ubiquitous in our lives. It is omnipresent. We all rely on it, but there is no control over the content and the algorithm, and it is having a serious impact on our children. I continue to meet a number of parents, including representatives of organizations now led by parents, who are advocating that kids should not have access to all those things. This is a valid concern. As a parent, I am concerned about it. I am really happy that, as parliamentarians, we are addressing this important issue.

I want to thank all my constituents in Ottawa Centre for taking the time to fill out the survey we circulated and for giving me this important information so I can be a strong champion for their point of view. We need to make sure the legislation not only passes but would actually be stronger and would protect our children.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague outlined the concerns of his constituents. I imagine that most of them would be happy about the idea of having legislation that would protect their children online. I think the vast majority of Canadians, of course, want that.

The question with the legislation, however, is, who would kids be protected from? Which platforms would be scoped in? Would Facebook, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat be scoped in? The legislation does not actually state that. It says that is yet to be determined in the regulations that we can expect at some date in the future. These types of decisions would be made behind closed doors rather than by elected officials in the House.

I am curious if the member could indicate how that would be determined. Which services would be scoped in, and which services would be allowed to continue to allow predatory practices with regard to our young people? Clearly, not all would be held accountable.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her very thoughtful comment and feedback on this important issue. I will start by saying that naming specific platforms may be problematic because legislation needs to be agnostic. What we really need to focus on is the technology and the algorithms that continue to evolve. Some companies, such as Facebook and Instagram, that exist today may not exist tomorrow. We need to write a piece of legislation that passes the test of time, so to speak, so I think our focus really should be on the harms and how to reduce their impact. That is why the regulator would be really important, because it could do the analysis to ensure that the regulations would address the harms we are trying to address here.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. colleague two quick questions.
Would it have been appropriate to extend the bill's scope to cover things like online gaming? How can we ensure that people under the age of 16 comply with the bill's provisions?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for those very important questions.

The second question is the one I was trying to address. It is one thing to say that the age is 16, but the enforcement of the rule is extremely important. That is one of the conversations I have had with my constituents that came up again and again. We can set up a lot of rules, but if the rules are not followed or enforced, they become meaningless. That is a concern I bring. I want to make sure the legislation would have a meaningful way of addressing that concern. I think that ideas and suggestions from all of us would make that happen. We do not want to create a black market, so to speak, for young people to find a back door to get to these types of things.

We all have been young, and we know how creative we could be if we wanted something. However, this is not a new experience for us. There are restrictions on the use of alcohol and tobacco, on driving, and those types of things, so we know how to do this right and should think about how we can enforce the age of 16 thoroughly to get it right.

Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the speech by my colleague from Ottawa Centre. I really appreciated the fact that he reached out to his constituents in different ways. I have done the same thing in my riding. I talked to the youth council, for instance. Young people in my riding told me that they strongly support stricter regulations governing the use of social media. They also talked about the many benefits of not being constantly active on social media.
I would like to know whether my colleague has done similar research with young people. How do the youth in his riding feel about regulations governing social media?

Mr. Speaker, I also spoke with my youth council on this important issue. What is funny is that there is a group of young people who do want strict regulations because they believe there are concerns with respect to social media. They want to be responsible users, and they want help from government regulators. Then there are other young people who want us to leave them alone. We need to find the right balance and the enforcement that would help reduce the harms regarding social media.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise to speak to this piece of legislation today. I have been thinking for some time about the issues raised by the legislation, in my capacity as shadow minister for mental health and wellness and in working with many stakeholders who are very concerned about the impact of social media on our kids.

To start, I am actually going to talk about something from my own experience that I think speaks to the very things we are talking about today. A few months ago, my mom was having a fairly minor surgery. One night as I was getting ready for bed, I thought I should text my mom to find out how her surgery went. The next morning, for whatever reason, I was about to text her about something else. I opened up my phone and realized I had never texted my mom the night before to ask her about her surgery. What I had done was open my phone with the full intention of sending a text, but I saw an Instagram notification, just that little dot on the Instagram logo that we cannot ignore, and clicked on something that was not important at all.

Instagram was just getting my attention, as it does. I spent probably an hour scrolling reels on Instagram, and none of those reels was important. The types of reels that get my attention on Instagram, generally, are fantastic sports plays set to great music. Certain comedians also get my attention, so my algorithm has Nate Bargatze, Jimmy Carr and other comedians. It also has videos that explain things through AI-generated songs that are kind of funny and maybe clever, maybe not filled with really accurate information. I do not know.

The other thing, though, that I notice about my algorithm is that it is filled with some things that are not so light. Recently, oftentimes, my feed would be filled with crash videos, sometimes plane crash videos. I fly a lot, and for whatever reason, if I see a piece of video or something like that, I will linger on it maybe a little longer than I should. I have noticed recently that my feed is filled with RIP content about people who have recently passed away. In retrospect, I know why that has happened. I believe in the JFK quote “Things do not happen. Things are made to happen.”

There is a reason why I see what I see. It is that a few prominent people whom I followed have passed away in recent times, and I read the stories about them. It was enough to feed my algorithm, and now what has happened is that my algorithm has way more content related to sadness and death than it used to have. What this has done is manipulated my natural love for people, my natural empathy for people, and has replaced that with a kind of rumination on tragedy, I would say.

One other comment is that on X, there is the ability, in some cases, to say, “I am not interested in this.” I have a specific ad that keeps popping up on X, a series of ads. I have clicked “not interested in this” at least four or five times, but they just keeps coming anyway. I cannot get rid of them.

What does that look like for kids? I think that is the question we have to answer today. It is one thing as a 57-year-old to be drawn into social media. I would not phrase it as an addiction for me right now, but it definitely is something that is very compelling and takes me away from things I care about doing. What does that look like for a 13- 14- or 15-year-old? They might sit down to look something up on their phone to do some homework or study for something, or maybe there is something that would just be interesting that adds value to their life, or they are texting a friend to make plans, but they get locked into some kind of notification or addictive scrolling session that might last an hour, or two or three hours, when they were just going on their phone to make plans with their friends to do something in person.

What does the content look like for kids? Too often, we are hearing that the content that our kids are seeing on there might be related to eating disorders or to the way that someone ought to look. It might be related, in many cases now, to gambling. Maybe it is just fun games at first, but it does not take very long before the algorithm starts to feed them gambling ads. Pornography is another thing that is drawing many kids in.

There is a question that we have to ask ourselves, because some people might have a conversation. I think there are some legitimate conversations around free speech in the debate. It will be interesting to see when we go to committee and hear from experts on the impact of other parts of the bill as they relate to free speech. However I would say, for the social media part, for me personally as I am looking at this, I do not see the issue of whether a 15-year-old should have access to social media as a free speech issue. In my view, 15-year-olds are not equipped to be signing contracts with social media behemoths and signing away access to their attention, which is what is happening.

It is not a coincidence that we are all seeing what we see on our social media feeds. It is not a coincidence that kids are seeing what they are seeing on their social media feeds. People are paying for them to see what they are seeing on their social media feeds, and the more time they spend on their devices, the more money someone makes in the background. That is an issue. Again, I do not believe that 15-year-olds are equipped to be entering into contracts that they do not fully understand and that tie them into seeing things that they did not expect to see and do not understand why they are seeing them.
I have a quote from C.S. Lewis that I love, and I think it kind of highlights where we are right now. He said:

Quote.QuotePara: We all want progress. But progress means getting nearer to the place where you want to be. And if you have taken a wrong turning then to go forward does not get you any nearer. If you are on the wrong road progress means doing an about-turn and walking back to the right road and in that case the man who turns back soonest is the most progressive man.

Content.ParaText: I want to think about the place we want to be, which C.S. Lewis talks about. I think we all want to be in a place where our kids can thrive, where we all can thrive, where we all can flourish and where we all can live up to our potential. I like to think of a world where our kids can play like we used to play.

Jonathan Haidt's work has been raised in a lot of the conversations around social media age limits particularly, of course. He has four norms that he points to, in terms of his work. He talks not only about a social media age limit, but also about a restriction on smartphones in schools, which provinces across this country have enacted. He talks about parents deciding to delay smartphone access for their kids to 14 years old. The fourth norm is more play in the real world. There is incredible research being done on the power of play in the real world.

I think of my friend Lenore Skenazy and her work on free-range kids, and Mariana Brussoni, a Canadian who does incredible work on unstructured play and the power of risky play. If we are going to go down a road with less social media access for kids, we have to have alternatives for our kids to undertake. I would say, as a country, one thing that we have to look at is where the spaces are where our kids can get outside and play, so more green space, but more green space where kids are safe to explore like we used to explore.

I know my time is running short right now. I am very much looking forward to this bill getting to committee. I think there are some legitimate concerns that folks would have about the bill that relate to fairly undefined powers of a regulator, the impact of some of the freedom of speech provisions within the bill that are not related necessarily to a social media age limit, and others.
Right now, I look forward to questions, but I really look forward to the conversations that are going to happen at committee on the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening closely to the member opposite's speech, and as a parent of an 18-year-old and a 20-year-old, I really agree with pretty much everything that he had to say here. That is a rare occurrence in this House. One of the things that I think about quite often is that my kids grew up with social media from day one, so the amount of data and information that has been collected from their lives when they are posting and when they are contributing on those platforms is really concerning. We see dystopian movies where targeted ads follow people around. I think some of the members' comments about unstructured play, getting outside and touching grass are also really important for youth.
I would like to know his comments on what he is hearing from other parents.

Mr. Speaker, that is a great question. Of course, I assume we have all been lobbied by the unplugged folks who are so passionate about this issue on behalf of their kids, which I think is more than 10,000 strong in terms of the impact. We have all gone back to our constituencies and talked to people.

In relation to the privacy issues the member raises, I want to give kudos to the member for Lethbridge who has consistently, as we have been having this conversation, been raising those issues. I expect they will be significantly raised in the committee as well.

Again, I come back to my focus and the work I have been doing and intend to be doing. There is a real power to play, and in order to make room for play, getting off or reducing time on our devices is going to be critical.

Mr. Speaker, when one looks at the legislation, the many implications it could have become pretty clear. If the government wants to regulate certain online platforms, for instance, it has to include some form of education for young people. It also means taking action on content that may differ depending on whether one is francophone or anglophone.

What I find especially unfortunate is that the bill does not include any obligation for the federal government to consult with the provinces or seek any kind of alignment, particularly with Quebec, which is a distinct society and has a different culture.
Would my colleague agree that the government has missed the mark a bit with the one-size-fits-all measures set out in the bill? That said, I completely agree on the importance of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of Parliament from Alberta, I would share those thoughts. Obviously, if the committee is given a strong enough mandate and enough time to study this piece of legislation, provinces will have a chance to weigh in, either at committee or by sending comments to the committee, and I think that would be really important.

It is important to me, more than almost any other piece of legislation I have seen, that Parliament, through the committee process right now, take the time to get this right. There are many legitimate concerns that have been raised, and it is very important that the committee that undertakes this study take the time to really hear those concerns and get it right.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his passionate speech and the incredible work he has done on this file over years, if not a decade, as a member of Parliament.

Bill C-34 does not outline the types of design features that should be put in place by platforms in order to keep kids safe. That is going to be determined later on. Given the member's tremendous amount of research and expertise in this area, I wonder if there are two or three design features he would hope to see come out of the regulatory framework that would be created.

Mr. Speaker, when we take a look at the different design features, such as infinite scroll, one of the conversations we need to have, and this is broader than just children, is on some transparency around why we see what we see. I think, for all of us, that is a huge issue. We just take what is given to us and go on to the next thing, and we do not know why we are seeing what we see. Some transparency around that is tremendously important. Again, this will probably be one of the key things that the committee looks at from witnesses who—
We will have to hear the rest at another time.
Resuming debate, the hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jacques Ramsay (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to the safe social media act. This topic holds considerable interest for many people in my riding of La Prairie—Atateken. I sincerely thank everyone who shared their views with me.

I want to start by addressing a reality that is quite familiar to families in my riding. In Candiac, Saint‑Constant, Kahnawake and other communities across the country, the first thing that many young people see on a screen in the morning and the last thing they see at night is an app. These services have real and undeniable benefits. They provide information, bring people closer together, and offer an outlet for creativity. However, they also expose our children to risks that we would never tolerate in other circumstances. The numbers are clear: One in four young people aged 12 to 17 say they have been cyber-bullied. Reports to police concerning online child sexual exploitation are increasing dramatically. In 2023‑24, the RCMP received over 100,000 reports in Canada alone in a single year.

Young people harmed in this way are much more likely to suffer from mental health issues, including suicidal ideation. Fourteen years ago, Amanda Todd took her own life because she was a victim of sextortion and cyber-bullying. Since then, two bills addressing online harm have died on the Order Paper. Victims and their families tell us that they have waited too long, and they are right. For a time, we hoped that the companies would take the necessary steps to keep our youth safe, but Canadians' trust has eroded. Their voluntary action has never kept pace with the scale, speed and severity of the harm caused. In addition to individuals' predatory behaviour, there are also design flaws, algorithmic recommendations, autoplay and infinite scroll. These are engineering choices that amplify harmful content. Worse still, today, AI chatbots are forming unhealthy, sustained relationships with young people, sometimes during the most difficult times of their lives. Tumbler Ridge is one example.

Bill C-34 is based on a simple principle: The people who design these services must be held accountable for the risks they create. The bill establishes two pieces of legislation: the digital safety act and the digital safety commission of Canada act. Allow me to outline their key provisions.

First, there is a duty to protect children. All regulated services will be required to integrate safe design features and implement age restrictions. As for social media, the government has provided that children must be at least 16 years old to have an account. However, the commission can grant exceptions to platforms that demonstrate that they have implemented and maintained sufficient protections for children. In other words, we are not closing the door. We are setting a standard.

Access to pornographic content must also be restricted using adequate age verification and age estimation measures. This responds to a call for action from our communities. In the spring, digital entrepreneurs and experts from Quebec, including some from my riding, launched an online initiative called AgeStandard, which calls for the enforcement of the 16-year-old age limit on social media. Thousands of people have signed the petition. Their message is simple: A check box has never protected a child. They are right.

Second, there is a duty to remove two types of content that do not belong anywhere: child sex abuse material and intimate images shared without consent, including sexual deepfakes. Social media platforms will be required to make such content inaccessible within 24 hours of it being flagged or reported, through a notice and appeal process. For a victim, every hour counts.

Third, there is a duty to act responsibly. Platforms will have to mitigate the risk of exposure to seven categories of harmful content, including content that induces a child to harm themselves, content used to bully a child, content that foments hatred, content that incites violence, and violent extremism content. They will have to provide simple tools for blocking, reporting and labelling synthetic content, and a readily available resource person.

Fourth, the bill establishes rules governing AI chatbots. If I am not mistaken, this is a world first. As soon as a user expresses suicidal thoughts or the intention to self-harm or hurt others, the service must immediately interrupt its interaction with the user and direct the user toward crisis intervention services that permit the user to interact with a human being. The chatbot may not pose as a human being or a professional, nor use manipulative engagement techniques to maintain an emotional attachment that causes the user to withdraw socially.

Fifth, the bill provides for greater transparency. Each regulated service must submit a digital safety plan containing information on the risks, the measures implemented and their effectiveness. Accredited researchers will be able to access the data. The days when platforms had to be taken at their word are over.

Lastly, the digital safety commission of Canada will be created and equipped with real technical expertise to develop standards, conduct audits, receive public complaints and impose penalties. Penalties for violations could be up to 3% of gross global revenue or $10 million. Convictions on indictment could lead to fines of up to 5% or $20 million, whichever is greater. For companies of this size, this is what sets a recommendation apart from a requirement.

Colleagues in this House, experts and citizens have raised serious concerns that deserve to be examined. First, there is a concern about freedom of expression. In my opinion, freedom of speech is not affected. For example, this bill does not apply to private messaging. It does not require platforms to proactively monitor everything that is being posted. It concerns these services' design and risk management. That is a fundamental difference.

We have also heard concerns about privacy and age verification. I share those concerns. Nobody here wants Canadians to have to hand over a piece of ID to watch a video. Where necessary, this verification should be done automatically. It will need to be properly regulated. This is something the committee will need to look at closely, particularly with the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.

I also want to acknowledge the sustained effort put in by Senator Julie Miville-Dechêne, whose bill, Bill S-209, has passed in the Senate and is now before the House. It aims to restrict young people's access to online pornography. Both bills have the same goal, and I hope the work done in committee will result in a consistent set of clear rules on age verification, rather than trying to impose two parallel systems on the same platforms. There is a way to do just that.

Some have said that too many details are being left to the regulations. That is a valid criticism, but as we know, technology evolves faster than we legislate. That is why it makes sense to enshrine the principles, obligations and penalties in law and to entrust the technical details to an expert body that can adapt as needed. There will be an opportunity at the committee stage to clarify what needs to be in the legislation itself.

Lastly, efforts are also under way elsewhere. The National Assembly of Quebec examined the effects of screen time on young people and focused on the role of schools and on support for families. Our bill addresses this issue by seeking to regulate global platforms. This is where the federal Parliament has a role to play. Platforms have a duty toward the children who use them, and that duty must be enshrined in law. I sincerely believe that the safety of our children is non-negotiable, as the minister said earlier.
The survivors have issued a call to us: If this bill is intended to build a safer digital future, then let it be built together with them. I urge all my colleagues to heed this call.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his interesting speech.

In its charter statement, the Department of Justice recognizes that the bill engages freedom of expression guaranteed under section 2(b) and the right to equality guaranteed under section 15 because it makes a distinction based on age, as well as the right to privacy under section 8 because the age verification or age estimation measures may require the collection of personal information.
What strikes me is that the charter statement is based on guidelines that will be developed later by the commission, on future regulations, and on an exemption for services that provide—
I must interrupt the hon. member to give the parliamentary secretary the opportunity to respond.

Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question, and I thank my colleague for asking it. I am a big believer in technological advances. The AgeStandard initiative that I mentioned earlier is suggesting that age verification be done by analyzing facial features, without seeking to identify the individual, or in other words, an automated age verification process that does not collect any personal information. That is just one example of what could be used. I think that members will have the opportunity in committee to examine charter compliance, which must always come first. I think it is possible to do that with Bill C-41 and the charter.
Mr. Speaker, when the Standing Committee on Canadian Heritage considered the issue, it adopted the following recommendation:

Quote.QuotePara: That the Government of Canada, in addressing the effects of influencers and social media on children and adolescents—and while recognizing the jurisdiction and primacy of the provinces in matters relating to social services and youth protection—adopt an asymmetrical and flexible approach.

Content.ParaText: I would like to ask my hon. colleague how, with Bill C-34, the government is taking an asymmetrical and flexible approach that recognizes the jurisdiction and primacy of Quebec and the provinces and how the government consulted and worked with Quebec and the provinces on this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think the two approaches are complementary. I have been watching the work of the Quebec National Assembly. It has focused on the effects of screen use in school, how families can better support their children, and specific health and education issues. I believe that Bill C‑41 addresses problems created by global platforms. I also believe the federal government has a fundamental role to play in establishing appropriate standards while giving platforms an opportunity to adapt. If they do so, then there will be no need for age verification. If they do not, I think it is our duty to intervene. I think this approach is in line with what almost all Quebeckers want.
Mr. Speaker, this bill does something very important: Anything that is currently illegal in the real world will also be illegal in the digital world. How can we ensure compliance with our laws?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague just made a very important point. Bill C‑41 does what is being done elsewhere. It regulates things that are not allowed, such as bullying and sexual exploitation. Basically, we need to recognize that online life is just as important in this day and age. We are doing that by introducing regulations that will evolve as technology evolves.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour and a pleasure to rise in the House as the voice of Calgary Midnapore. I am so grateful for my citizens. Many of my citizens, including my parents, of course, and myself, are parents. When we talk about being a parent, we may have many other titles and roles in our lives. We may be a sister or a cousin. In our work, we have many roles. We may be a colleague, perhaps a subordinate or even a leader, a boss, someone who has to take the care and responsibility of others into consideration. I know that any parent, not only in Calgary Midnapore but across Canada, would agree that there is nothing more important than their role as a parent and the safety of their children. We all love our children. I cannot think of anything more dear or precious to me than my son, and I know all parents feel this way about their children.

It should be known to Canadians that protecting kids online is non-negotiable for Conservatives. However, good intentions require sound mechanisms. We must be focused on holding tech giants accountable and empowering parents, not expanding government bureaucracy. As this bill moves to committee, we will scrutinize its provisions to ensure that it delivers real protection for children. As a parent, I want nothing more than that for our children and for the parents of Canada.

Online harms are a real problem, and the problem is twofold. Number one, children are exposed to addictive platforms. I see this in my household, and when friends come over, all the time. There is inappropriate content, exploitation and many other harms. Secondly, parents are overwhelmed by rapidly changing technology and fighting an uphill battle against big tech. This was never more prevalent than during COVID, when all parents across the nation all of a sudden had to become IT consultants, so to speak, as they navigated schooling for their children during that difficult time.

These are real problems. According to Statistics Canada, one in four children aged 12 to 17 has experienced cyber-bullying, and police reported online child sexual exploitation incidents reaching 16,905 in 2024, up 347% from 2014. Cyber-victimization is also associated with serious mental health outcomes, including suicidal ideation and attempts. Canada has experienced the devastating impacts and real-world consequences of online harms. The tragic case of Amanda Todd, who died by suicide after experiencing sextortion and cyber-bullying, illustrates the devastating impact these harms can have on young people. In addition, I have two examples from my home province of Alberta.

Dated September 25, the headline on the first article states, “After 2 youths stalked on Snapchat, review your kid’s settings, police urge”. The article reads, “Police in Alberta are urging parents to check the location settings on their children’s social media and communication apps after two youth allegedly being sexually exploited in Edmonton were followed to their homes.” This is outlining the threats. “'The victims reported that they complied out of extreme fear for their safety and the safety of their family,'” again outlining the threats.

The article continues: “The suspect allegedly tracked the victim’s location via Snapchat and travelled to their family home. ALERT said they allegedly knew both the victims’ home address and what school they attended.” This is the type of threat that exists as a result of social media. That is one example from my home province of Alberta.

The headline on the second article says, “Edmonton teens, 14, charged after AI used to make sexualized images of classmates”. The article states, “Two Edmonton junior high students are facing child sexual exploitation charges for allegedly using AI to generate sexualized images of classmates. Such charges are only the tip of the iceberg in an emerging area of online child sex abuse, police say, adding it remains difficult to hold AI platforms themselves accountable.”

Problems for children are many, and children spend a large portion of their lives online. For today's youth, digital platforms are not separate from everyday life. This is where they socialize, build relationships, access information, express themselves and, increasingly, interact with AI. As a result, what happens online can have profound real-world consequences, including exposure to cyber-bullying, sexual exploitation, self-harm and eating disorder content, violence, and other harmful material.

Children are vulnerable to the ways that platforms are designed. Platform features, such as recommendation algorithms, push notifications, endless scrolling and autoplay can repeatedly direct youth towards content that keeps them engaged. These design choices can amplify exposure to harmful material and make it difficult for young users to disengage. At the same time, AI chatbots and digital companions are becoming increasingly integrated into the platforms used by young people, creating new and largely untested risks.

In addition to problems for children, there are problems for parents. Parents cannot solve the problem alone, and they are asking for help. They can set boundaries, monitor devices and talk to children about online safety. We have done all of this in my home, but parents cannot control how platforms and algorithms recommend content, prevent strangers from contacting their children or remove harmful material at scale.

Parents need technology companies and governments to share responsibility for creating a safer online environment for children. We do not ask parents to enforce car seat standards or alcohol laws by themselves, and online safety should be no different. In fact, according to an Angus Reid survey, 75% of Canadians, and 70% of parents with children in the home, support banning social media for youth under 16.
I will give an example in my province of such legislation. This legislation exists not only in Alberta but also across other provinces in the federation. On June 17, 2024, it was decreed:

Quote.QuotePara: Parents, teachers, students and our education partners were clear that the use of personal mobile devices and social media in the classroom was of concern. We're taking a measured approach to protect students by restricting the use of personal mobile devices during instructional time to reduce distractions and bullying, maximize learning time and support student mental health.

Content.ParaText: This is one province that has taken an approach to such threats and such risks, because the threats, as I said, are very much real.

We need to consider also the duties of operators, because these operators have a duty to protect our children. They should require social media services and chatbot services to implement design features respecting the protection of children, as per future regulations. They should require social media services to implement age verification estimation to prevent users who are under 16 from setting up or maintaining accounts. As well, they should require regulated services that provide access to pornographic material to implement age verification or age estimation to prevent children from getting access to these platforms. These operators have a duty to act responsibly. They should require social media services and chatbots to assess and mitigate the risks associated with several categories of harmful content. As well, they have a duty to make certain that certain content is inaccessible and require social media services to take down content that sexually victimizes children.
Our Conservative principles regarding online safety are clear, and as a parent and as a mother, I ask the government to consider them.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the member's speech. I am really glad that there is a lot of consensus across all parties on this bill.

This is so essential in my role, and I have heard briefing after briefing. We have talked about a lot of different crimes, but on the harm that is happening to our children online, as the member pointed out, we have seen an increase of over 400% over the last decade, and even year on year, about a 64% increase in luring children online.

I want to thank the RCMP for all the work it does to combat this issue, but holding social media companies liable is a really important part of this piece. I want to hear the members' comments on reporting to police services.

Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to hear my colleague across the aisle indicate that she believes holding social media platforms accountable for the safety of our children is important. It indicates to me that she recognizes that her role as a government member is to create this environment and enforce it with social media platforms.

In this moment, I think that Canadians and parents across Canada are uncertain if the government is willing to do the difficult things and stand up to big social media regarding keeping our children safe. I will take her words and her commentary as an acceptance of the responsibility of government to hold social media companies to account.
Mr. Speaker, indeed, the time has come to deal with this situation.
My question is this. In our society, which level of government is ultimately responsible for protecting young people? I am thinking of the young people in Quebec, for example.
Would my colleague agree that, while legislation is needed, it is up to the Quebec nation to have a serious discussion about these legislative choices?

Mr. Speaker, I think it is everyone's responsibility to protect young people. I think that is probably the most important aspect of the bill. Protecting young people is up to me, as a parent, but it is also up to the government and companies. I hope the government will accept its responsibility in that regard.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of the member's speech, she mentioned that, although the bill is well-intentioned and there are some good elements to it, one of her concerns was the potential of adding additional bureaucracy, which could slow down some of the things we are trying to accomplish with the bill, certainly in ensuring that the tools are there for our law enforcement to act on these things.
Could the member build on some of her concerns regarding other elements of the bill, including the bureaucracy, that are a concern to our stakeholders?
Mr. Speaker, that is an excellent question.

There are three concerns when it comes to bureaucracy. The first, of course, is that bureaucracy always has a price, and with this government, it is a very big one. Second, a bureaucracy allows the government and the ministers to deflect responsibility back onto the bureaucracy when they themselves should be taking responsibility, especially in a situation where something so precious as our children is involved. Finally, a bureaucracy gives unelected officials power to harm people. I am very concerned about the bureaucratic aspects of this, because as we can see, the risks are many.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the fact that the government is looking at regulating social media among young people. I also commend the leadership shown by the Premier of Quebec, who was one of the first people in Quebec to raise this issue. Other western countries are also considering this.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!
I think I am bothering one of my colleagues. I hope it is not just because I am speaking French.
Some countries are taking a bold approach. Others are waiting to see what kind of legislation is passed and may take their cue from what we do here.

I am certainly not the only one who sees people my age in my circle of friends who go into a trance as soon as they open Instagram or TikTok, although that app is not as popular as it once was. Of course, there are also the short videos on Facebook.

The tech giants understand human nature. They understand the weaknesses of the human mind, how our attention span works and, most importantly, how to keep us hooked. They know how to get our attention and feed us content that can make us lose all sense of time. I do not think there is a single person here who has not experienced this. In fact, many of the people who created these platforms admit that they too fall victim to their own tactics and this game. Our partners, our children, our friends—all are susceptible.

The difference is that we are adults and we have free will. In theory, we are equipped to understand these dangers but, as with any addiction, it is difficult to break free, especially once we have lost track of time.

Now, let us think about all the 12-year-old boys and girls who are just starting junior high. Their parents buy them a cellphone because they want to keep track of where they are going and because junior high brings with it a new kind of freedom. Parents also want to be able to contact their children. There are all sorts of good reasons for these kids to have cellphones. We are no longer talking about the old flip phones that no one wanted to send text messages on because it took too long. Kids can now get on the Internet with their phones. They have access to social media. There are apps to block social media, but let us be serious. Young people want a digital presence. It is important to point that out. We obviously have to keep up with the times. That is why Bill C-34 is so important.

Digital communication is at now at the centre of our lives. If we do not regulate it, we are leaving young people to navigate these platforms alone, platforms where they may be exposed to cyber-bullying, content that is not age appropriate and mechanisms designed to keep them online into the wee hours of the morning. I remember when I was old enough to get my driver's licence, I was told to save my money so that I could buy myself a car. A car does not come for free and it comes with rules. It is important to know how to navigate this digital world because, even though it may be intangible, there are still public health and safety issues to consider.

There is also something that is not as easy to pick up on among young people: young people who isolate themselves, who become withdrawn and whose mental health could be affected by online pressure and interactions. When I talk about interactions, I think about the fact that every second we are in front of a screen adds up. Screen time could even take the place of time spent sleeping. We also know that the amount of time spent doing physical activity and being physically present with others is decreasing. We all know that sedentary lifestyles can be harmful to physical health. In addition, online pressure and interactions can take a heavy toll on mental health. These effects are real and cannot be ignored. The pandemic reminded us just how much young people need to interact with others in order to learn to socialize. When so many of our interactions are happening only online, socialization becomes more difficult and some people may withdraw into themselves.

I am sure that my very attentive colleagues agree. We must learn from what is happening now and help both current and future generations develop a healthy relationship with digital tools without becoming dependent on them.

On social media, young people see digitally enhanced bodies and carefully curated lives. Success often appears effortless, but comparing ourselves to those images can leave us feeling that we are not attractive enough, popular enough or successful enough. In fact, a study of just over 21,000 youth aged 10 to 17 in six countries, including Canada, found that 55% were dissatisfied with their appearance. One could argue that not many of us are satisfied, but dissatisfaction tends to increase as time spent on social media increases.

We already use this approach for other products. For instance, tobacco advertising, packaging and warnings are regulated. The same goes for cannabis. There is a minimum age, and marketing aimed at young people is tightly restricted. With social media, the risks are different, but the principle is the same: Protect people and prevent harm through regulations. Limiting young people's access is therefore a public health measure, not arbitrary control. We need to make that distinction.

We in the Bloc Québécois think it is normal and preferable for laws to adapt quickly to technological changes. Our laws are lagging far behind, and this gap must be closed to keep up with the accelerating pace of AI. Even the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has called for rules to protect children across all social media. These are the rules we are being called upon to discuss and debate as we study Bill C-34. I hope that the discussions will be very constructive once the bill passes this stage and that the committee will come up with effective measures to keep our young people on the right track.

What rules should we bring in to regulate social media and protect young people? Which level of government within the Canadian federation has the jurisdiction to address this challenge? These are questions that need to be asked as this bill proposes a federal regulatory framework for social media and chatbots.

This bill would also impose a number of duties on digital platforms, including a duty to protect minors and to make certain content inaccessible. This will, in fact, help to educate parents. The bill places obligations on these platforms, including requirements to remove content depicting sexual victimization and non-consensual intimate images. It proposes a range of principles, obligations and enforcement mechanisms aimed at holding digital platforms accountable, protecting minors and ensuring online safety.

The Bloc Québécois supports these objectives and sees the positive side of a number of the principles and proposed solutions. However, each of these measures will require careful examination. I repeat that, in committee, I hope we will ensure that our decisions are guided by science, facts and research, and not simply guided by assumptions or, I dare say, partisan politics. As the Bloc Québécois has always maintained, we must also ensure that the federal government does not encroach on areas of jurisdiction that belong to Quebec and the provinces.

In conclusion, in 2024 and 2025, Quebec's National Assembly established a Select Committee on the Impacts of Screens and Social Media on Young People's Health and Development. Let us draw on the work of our counterparts to ensure a healthy digital environment for our young people.
Mr. Speaker, I truly appreciated the speech by my colleague from Laurentides—Labelle.

I must acknowledge that the Bloc Québécois has consistently advocated strong measures to combat cyber-bullying and threats of all kinds directed at children. Those are values we share. In the case of this bill, many of its provisions are aimed at preventing the commission and perpetuation of criminal offences.
I want to know whether my colleague agrees that prevention should be one of the main objectives of a bill like this one.
Mr. Speaker, what a great question from my colleague.

I come from the community sector, a sector that is stretched thin in Quebec, and I know that prevention is key. Indeed, when we see the strategies being used by platforms that turn young people into zombies, we understand that safeguards need to be implemented. We need to invest more and develop a legislative framework that protects the physical and mental health of our young people.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate and thank my colleague and friend, the member for Laurentides—Labelle, for her great speech. The topic is important, and she addressed it with heartfelt conviction.
The issue covered by this bill touches on many areas of jurisdiction that belong to Quebec and the provinces, including social services, youth protection and other related sectors.
In my colleague's view, has the government worked closely enough with Quebec and the provinces on this matter? Did it adequately consult the other levels of government before introducing this bill?
Mr. Speaker, that is exactly the question we are asking.

We are perfectly comfortable with the bill and we hope it will pass into law. Once it is referred to committee, I hope that Quebec and the provinces will be consulted, considering the research they conducted, the evidence they gathered from scientists and the measures they implemented that we need to use for inspiration.
The government may have consulted the provinces to some degree, but a lot more such consultation is needed.
Mr. Speaker, I just want to thank our colleague for her speech.

I thank her for supporting the measures proposed by the Canadian government to protect young people and for recognizing that this is a shared responsibility. The Canadian government has a responsibility, including because social media has no borders.
It is an excellent recognition of the role of the Canadian government, which must act in collaboration with other players, of course.

Mr. Speaker, indeed, the new government at the National Assembly of Quebec includes people who are very competent. I must say that the MNA for the Laurentians, Anne Nguyen, has a great deal of expertise.
I cannot wait for the bill to see the light of day because it is high time this law was implemented quickly, especially given that artificial intelligence is so pervasive in our lives.

Mr. Speaker, in her speech, my colleague said that she hoped her colleagues were listening attentively. We certainly were, because right after, she talked about how it is important to protect the younger generation.

In that spirit, under the framework of the bill, instead of an outright ban on social media, it would allow certain platforms to be exempt from the age verification obligations if they can show that they have a robust safety plan in place.

I want to know what my colleague thinks of this approach. Rather than being subject an outright ban, platforms would be given an opportunity to implement preventative measures. What does she think about that?

Mr. Speaker, in less than 30 seconds, I will say that the government needs to consult public safety stakeholders and every province and territory. I think the government will then get feedback that would likely be very positive.
That said, I would remind the House that it is also important for the government to focus on its own affairs.

SubjectOfBusiness.SubjectOfBusinessQualifier: Bill C-41—Proposal to Apply Standing Order 69.1

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I rise to respond to the point of order raised by the member for Elgin—St. Thomas—London South respecting the application of Standing Order 69.1 to Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguards act.

Bill C-41 proposes substantive amendments to the Criminal Code to deal with medical assistance in dying. As a result of these amendments, other acts of Parliament would be amended as a consequence for the sole purpose of the amendments made to the Criminal Code respecting the medical assistance in dying regime.

Paragraph 12.50 of the fourth edition of the House of Commons Procedure and Practice states in relation to the division of an omnibus bill, “The Standing Orders define an omnibus bill as a bill intended to modify, repeal or enact more than one law with no common thread or which concern unrelated topics.”

The stated bill, Bill C-41, deals with the singular issue of medical assistance in dying and no unrelated topics. The member has clearly acknowledged this in his intervention when he stated, “I recognize that these matters concern medical assistance in dying.”

To demonstrate how closely intertwined the two medical assistance in dying matters addressed in the bill are linked, I would draw the attention of members to subclause 5(9), which states, “A mental illness is not an illness or disease in respect of which an advance request may be made.”
The bill clearly deals with medical assistance in dying as a common element and theme and contains no unrelated provisions dealing with unrelated matters.

Taken to its logical end, if what the member is proposing were to be accepted, each and every bill the government introduces that contains a common element and deals with no unrelated matters could be subject to multiple votes at the second reading and third reading stages and would put the Speaker in an awkward position to classify bills according to how strongly some members feel about the subject matter contained therein.

I submit that the appropriate place for members to consider the clauses of the bill is at committee where, unlike at second reading, members may propose amendments or simply vote against clauses they oppose.

I conclude that Bill C-41, for which the substantive proposed amendments relate to the medical assistance in dying regime in the Criminal Code, does not in any way constitute an omnibus bill and, therefore, the application of Standing Order 69.1 does not apply. I would encourage the House to expeditiously refer the bill to committee where members can examine, consider and propose amendments to the individual clauses.
So noted.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there are many parents and grandparents in this room and listening who, I am sure, all want the same thing: to know that when our children or grandchildren go online, they are safe. We want our children to be able to talk to friends, learn new things, play games and research their interests without worrying that someone might be trying to exploit them, bully them or expose them to things they are not ready to see. For many parents, that peace of mind is hard to find.

Parents can do everything right. They can set rules for screen time, monitor what sites their children visit and even teach them about online harms and safety or what to do when they feel uncomfortable. What parents cannot control is what a social media site recommends to their child. They cannot personally review every single message that their child receives, and they cannot make a tech company remove harmful content just because it puts their child at risk. That is the challenge we are facing today.

Children are spending more of their time online than ever before. The risks they are facing change as fast as the technology does. One in four Canadian children between the ages of 12 and 17 has experienced cyber-bullying. In 2024, police reported that online child exploitation reached 16,905 children, up 347% from 2014. Behind those numbers are real families and real children who have real trauma from it. We have seen the consequences of online harm in cases like that of Amanda Todd.

As AI becomes more common and more integrated into our children's lives, we need to know where the responsibility lies when something goes wrong. This brings us to Bill C-34. The bill proposes responsibilities for social media companies and AI chatbots. It would require them to take steps to protect children and address harmful content. It would also establish the new digital safety commission of Canada to oversee compliance, investigate complaints and enforce the rules.

I think we can all agree that we want our children to be safe online. The question is, how do we get there? Good intentions are not enough. For too long, parents have been expected to manage these risks alone. We can think about how social media works for one second. What is recommended is not random. It is designed to keep people watching. It is designed for children to keep scrolling, the video playbacks to be played based on what they are viewing, and constant ads or continual use by children as they scroll through the platforms. These features can make it difficult for young people to put their phones down. It can also affect what content a child will see next.

Technology companies make decisions about how their products work, but they also need to take responsibility. Bill C-34 proposes requirements for safer design, but that raises a question. What does safer design mean, and how will we know what changes are working? Parents do not have the comfort to wait years to find out what these changes will bring. We need clear expectations, measurable results and a way to hold companies accountable when they fall short.

This brings me to another part of the bill, on age restrictions. Bill C-34 would require social media apps to verify age to prevent users under the age of 16 from having accounts. The intention is understandable. There are legitimate concerns about the effects of social media on young people. Many parents today are already doing what they can to limit or restrict social media use. My question is, what if a teenager is determined to still use these platforms? They may move to a site that is less known and has fewer safeguards. They may end up giving their parents even less visibility into what is happening. A restriction is only effective if it can be enforced and it keeps children safe in the process.

We also need to ask how this verification would work. If Canadians have to provide some sort of identification or other personal information to prove their age, how will that information be protected? We need to make sure that in the effort to protect our children, we do not create unnecessary risks for everyone, including our children. We also need to consider the role of parents. Parents know their children. They understand their needs better than anybody else, especially in ways the government cannot. A parent may decide that their 15-year-old is not ready for online activities, while another says that potentially theirs is.

We do not know this yet. Not all families will come to the same decision, and the law needs to account for how these rules would affect them. Parents cannot be expected to solve every single online problem on their own, and they have to be a part of this conversation. Online safety should be a shared responsibility. Yes, parents need the tools to help them make the best decisions for their own families, but big tech companies also need to do their part. The government must do its part as well.

Would these measures actually make children safer? Would tech companies be held accountable for the risks that these platforms create? Would parents have the tools needed to protect their children while their privacy is being respected? We need to have the answers as the bill moves forward.

Parents are asking for help, and technology companies should not be able to ignore the harms that their products are causing to children. Our responsibility is to make sure that the rules we put in place work to protect children and respect the rights of Canadians. At the end of the day, parents do not want another empty promise that the Internet will be safer. They need protections that actually work.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is really important that we recognize that Bill C-34 is all about protecting the children in Canada. It would complement the wonderful job that parents and guardians provide, but it recognizes that the Internet is seven days a week, 24 hours a day, and that there is harmful content there.

What we are hoping to see from the Conservative Party is support in principle for a digital safety commission so that when we have the regulations, they would actually be enforced with, potentially, things like fines. There has to be a consequence that gives the legislation teeth in its actions to protect our children. In principle, does the member support the legislation and, in particular, the commission?

Mr. Speaker, I wholeheartedly agree that we absolutely want to keep our children safe. The whole principle of the bill is keeping our children safe on the platforms they are continually using. Every single day, this is where they gather. It is where they play. We need to ensure that tech companies are held accountable. We also agree that this legislation needs to have real teeth in it, absolutely. One of the things, though, that I have received emails about is the commission's powers and accountability. These are the things we are going to need to discuss in committee moving forward.

Mr. Speaker, I am wondering whether my colleague shares my concern. As we have seen, the government has occasionally had a regrettable tendency to let the tech giants off easy. We need only think of the digital services tax or the levies, two areas where the government has backed down. We know that legislation like this is likely to displease platforms like Facebook. We also know how much influence these people can have on the U.S. President.
Does my colleague fear, as I do, that the government might end up backing down if the Americans were to exert economic pressure to persuade us not to go down this route?

Mr. Speaker, there is a piece in the legislation on the duties of operators, which would hold big tech accountable, and in there is the duty to act responsibly. It would require social media and these platforms and services like chatbots to assess and mitigate risks associated with seven categories of harmful content. Those categories are intimate content communicated without consent; content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor; content that induces a child to harm themselves; content used to bully a child; content that foments hatred; content that incites violence; and terrorism or violent extremism content.

A piece of this that we will have to look at when this moves to committee is ensuring that there would be true accountability by these content providers and that it is not just an illusion. As such, this is something that we will be talking about as this moves forward.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in the debate, the member was asked about support for the creation of a commission, which is part of the act. I do not think a part of this, like the commission, could be or is a complete answer to the question of online harms. Some online harms are criminal acts. When crimes are committed, the commission of crime is a matter for law enforcement, not a commission. I think it is really important that we examine all of the issues around this bill and that we get it right.
Does the member agree that there are many questions that a parliamentary committee needs to address? Does she think there is likely room for amendment?
