Bill C-34 changes all that. This bill is based on a simple idea: safety by design. I am going to list three duties that will help achieve that. First, there is the duty to protect children. We need age-appropriate safeguards built into the products. Companies need to mitigate addictive features, add warnings and provide safe search settings. I repeat: This is a duty that begins at the design stage. Second, there is the duty to act responsibly. Companies must identify and reduce risks, provide effective blocking and reporting tools, and label deepfakes and content created by AI. Canadians deserve to know what is real and what is not. Finally, there is the duty to make the most serious types of content inaccessible: child sexual abuse material and intimate images shared without consent. Once reported, such content must be removed within 24 hours. If the platform does nothing, the victim will no longer be alone. They can turn to the digital safety commission of Canada.

Chatbots need a crisis protocol. When a young person expresses an intention to harm themselves or others, the bot will no longer be able to simply continue the conversation. It will be required to refer the person to appropriate help. For social media, users will have to be at least 16 to open an account. However, the door is wide open for platforms to be granted an exemption if they can demonstrate that their service is safe for children. The message is simple: Platforms are welcome to seek an exemption if they can prove that their product is safe and truly reliable for users. I talked about it with my 14-year-old son. I told him that our government was planning on imposing a minimum age of 16 for the use of social media. It sparked quite a discussion, but my son eventually came around to the view that this objective was very noble, because protecting young people is so important.

All of this will be overseen by Canada's new digital safety commission, which will be independent and made up of three to five expert members. It will review the safety plans published by the platforms, handle complaints, support victims and have the power to impose fines of up to 3% of global revenues. I am hearing some concerns today. They are legitimate, and I want to address them frankly and clearly, but above all in a responsible manner.

With respect to freedom of expression, it is protected by the charter, and this bill does not restrict it. The bill covers seven categories of harmful content, each of which is deliberately narrowly defined. The bill does not cover debate, disagreement or criticism, even when expressed in the strongest possible terms. What is more, the commission will have no power to arrest anyone. With respect to privacy, private messaging is specifically excluded. Data collected for age verification purposes must be protected and then promptly destroyed. It can be used for only one purpose: to prevent harm.

This bill does not target what Canadians say. It focuses on how platforms are built. Seventy-seven per cent of the population wants us to take action, so that is what we are doing. Pediatricians want us to take action, and so does everyone else.

I will return to the image of the faint blue glow under the door. I do not long for a world without screens. That world is gone. Digital media offers a marvellous opportunity for our young people—if it is used right.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-34 would allow young people back onto social media platforms once providers meet the guidelines that would be established by the commission, but we do not know yet what those guidelines would require or whether they would be good enough to keep young people safe. Too often, big tech companies and their lobbyists are given a seat at the table when these decisions are made. Can the member assure the House that these guidelines would be developed independently of big tech companies and their lobbyists, with the safety of young people as their priority?

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his highly relevant question. We need to bear in mind who is going to sit on this commission. It will not be politicians or decision-makers from the House of Commons, but experts who, obviously, care about our children's future.

My colleague talked about age. Let me say again that the minimum age for social media will be 16. That is what the bill provides. Let me also say again that the commission will be composed of experts.
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate my colleague on his highly informative speech.
One of my concerns is that the digital platforms, social media, are multinational corporations that often seem prepared to flout the laws and regulations of the countries where they operate.

The Standing Committee on Industry and Technology conducted a study on fraud. We found that the platforms are slow to act on fraudulent advertising. They claim that they are doing everything they can, but even after fraudulent advertising is reported, it takes them days, if not weeks, to remove it. Once a bill like this is passed, does my hon. colleague believe that the digital platforms will co-operate, or might we still run into a few stumbling blocks?

Mr. Speaker, the short answer is yes. However, it is not just about cooperation. It is also an obligation, one that has to come with penalties. When obligations are imposed without accompanying penalties, then they are just a suggestion. That is not the intent of Bill C-34, quite the contrary. The bill aims to protect our children. Everyone knows as well as I do that protecting our children is essential. International companies will not stand in the way of the government's determination.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague for his speech and the extraordinary work he does to serve his constituents.

I would ask my colleague to tell the House and the parents and young people in his riding why it is important for us to adopt Bill C-34. What will this do to better protect Canadians, especially young Canadians?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague, who represents the riding neighbouring mine, for that great question.

It is very simple. As I mentioned, I have a 14-year-old son. We know full well that when a toy is dangerous, it is taken off the market and off of store shelves. My son spends most of his time in front of a screen. I think we need to address this issue much more seriously. I cannot ask parents in Bourassa and across Canada to monitor their children's online activities 24 hours a day, seven days a week. That is virtually impossible. However, the platforms have the means to do so, they have the algorithms to do so, and they must do just that.
Mr. Speaker, children need real protection online. Is Bill C‑34 the best solution? This method is not working in Australia.
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for asking her question in such elegant French. I appreciate it.

The unique thing about this bill is that it is a world first. It is a step forward, and I hope that everyone here will vote to support it. There are three aspects. Australia did not regulate all of the aspects I listed in my speech, including the issue of social media, AI and platforms, as well as safety by design.

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise on behalf of the people of Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. It is always an honour to speak in the House of Commons, but on this occasion, it is a particular honour.

Before I begin, I want to recognize and honour the life of Attilio Sirianni, who passed away last month in Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. He leaves behind his children Ferro, Teresa, Mario, Gino, Maria and Raffelina. I extend my deepest condolences to Attilio's family. May perpetual light shine upon him.

Before I get into my speech, I want to recognize the life of Angelo Carusi, who recently passed away in Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. Those who are left to mourn him include his father Tino, who I have gotten to know through the Colombo Lodge, our local Italian cultural centre; his son Angelo; and his siblings Augie, Ed and Rina. May perpetual light shine upon him. I extend my deepest condolences to the Carusi family.

When I was young and growing up, I basically spent my time watching baseball. I was a huge Blue Jays fan. Because I was on the west coast, the Blue Jays games would start at 4:30 p.m. every day. I would come home from school and that is essentially what I did. I had a 286 computer that I would use for word processing. My dot matrix printer was always there and always ready to help me out. I used that all the way until I was in my third year of university. In 1999, I think I got a Windows-based computer. That tells members how old I am. At the end of the day, the computer was a tool for work. I had terrible handwriting, so I would often type out my things. My mom was a legal assistant and could type about 60 or 70 words a minute, so I would sometimes conscript her into typing out my work assignments, for which I thank her. Things were simply different.

For instance, I have a background as someone who has worked extensively to combat Internet luring, but the luring of children, back when I was a child, was all done face-to-face. When people wanted to meet one another, they took out classified ads. The young people would read these ads and make fun of them. That was essentially how people met. Let us face it, kids were not generally responding to these ads. Luring takes place when somebody deliberately targets a child and, through that, attempts to lure the child into a relationship. It is almost never initiated by the child. That is why it is called luring. This is an area that I devoted a fair amount of my time to. It is no wonder, when we think about how much time kids spend online.

The Internet has changed a lot of things, but in some ways I think it has made the predatory world even more predatory. The anonymity of the Internet is something else. I remember attending a workshop about luring and the difficulties for children. We were told about all these social media vehicles where people did not even have to enter their name or email address and they could instantly go into a chat room and start talking to people, or do something that essentially was a crime immediately without any oversight. For far too long, it has been my view that service providers and social media providers have looked the other way.

When people look at the stats, they see that a number of crimes have skyrocketed. That is one of the reasons why I put forward my bill, Bill C-291, in the last Parliament, which received royal assent. I did that with the former member of what is now Kamloops—Shuswap—Central Rockies. The reason we put that bill forward to change the name of child pornography to child sexual abuse and exploitation material was to reflect the gravity of the offence.

If somebody were to look at a chart, what they would see for 2013 is this massive skyrocketing, probably by about 10 to 15 times, of the reporting of offences. That is not just because more predators were born in, say, 1993 or something, and the offences are now coming to fruition. The difference was a difference in reporting. For far too long, we saw organizations and providers essentially turning a blind eye, as in they knew that luring was happening and the Internet was an unsafe place, yet nothing was done.

In 2012, and I am proud to say this as a Conservative, the Conservative government imposed a positive obligation on service providers to report. People might ask what a positive obligation is. Most laws are negative obligations in criminal law or in traffic law. “Do not speed” is a negative obligation. Someone has to not do something. “Do not assault” is another example.

A positive obligation requires a person to do something. For instance, paying taxes is a positive obligation. This law imposed a positive obligation for service providers to report, and the numbers absolutely skyrocketed. It was not just that this was happening more; it was being detected more.

I recently went to the RCMP to meet with RCMP commissioner Duheme and deputy commissioner Larkin, as well as many others, many of whom are in the business of protecting children. I went with the member for Oxford. It was a great meeting. These are the unsung heroes, in my view, of our law enforcement community. The reason is that they deal with child sexual abuse and exploitation material, day in and day out. They do not get a reprieve. They are the ones who have to deal with it, so I want to give a shout-out to those people because they are not paid more to do this, yet they put their lives and mental health on the line so that others do not have to, as they protect our children.

This is all to say that this is a crucial area of law. The Internet, let us face it, is not a safe place. Where I would like to see things go and where I would actually challenge the government to go on this point is with respect to sentencing. We are talking about an Internet regulator, but so much of what concerns us in our discourse here in Bill C-34, what we are aiming to do, the pernicious and insidious harms, if we will, of kids being on the Internet, is actually already regulated by criminal law.

I think we should be looking at the sentencing. I will give an example. Internet luring began with a sentence of five years in jail, maximum. A maximum sentence is a sentence that can be imposed, but not must be imposed. It started at five years, and then it went to 10 years. As Conservatives, I am proud that we upped it to 14 years.

Bill C-299 is a private member's bill I tabled last Parliament. I believe sentencing should go to life in prison. I believe someone who offends against children for that offence, or for sexual interference, which is essentially the sexual assault of a child, because children cannot consent, should be liable to life. If someone touches a kid, they should see the inside of a jail cell. I have said it before and I will say it again: If I am ever in charge of making laws on the government side, I will not stop until sex offenders see the inside of a jail cell for a darn long time.

I know I am already running short on time just talking about this. It is an area of great passion for me. I really do think that we have to value the mental health of children. We really do. This is not something that I think only the Conservatives value or only the Liberals value. Let us be real. Everybody in here values the mental health of children. How we go about it is what we need to debate substantially. I would invite the government to consider thinking about the sentencing aspect.

Before I end, I want to reflect on the life of Iolanda Bartella, somebody from Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola who recently passed away. Iolanda leaves behind her sons Frank, Carmelo and Rob. I actually taught her granddaughter Kiely at law school in a class on sentencing, probably eight or nine years ago. Kiely is now a lawyer. I send my deepest condolences to the Bartella family. May perpetual light shine upon her.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague for speaking to Bill C-34. I always say crime is a non-partisan issue. My colleague and I sit together on the public safety committee and work together on so many bills that we passed last year.

In June, we worked on Bill C-22 in committee, which is on lawful access, and complementary legislation to Bill C-34. It would provide law enforcement agencies with additional tools to help solve these criminal issues and keep our children safe online.
With Bill C-34, our goal is to hold large social media companies accountable. Unfortunately, Bill C-22 was delayed by opposition members.

My question is as follows: Will my colleague and members of the opposition party commit to supporting Bill C-34's timely passage and ensuring that big tech companies will be kept accountable to keep our children safe?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for her question.
I practise my French with the member once in a while, and I have enjoyed sitting with her on the public safety committee.

There is a lot to go through here, and I am not going to be able to get through it all, but one of the things I want to say about Bill C-22, and I talked about Internet luring, is that my life in my former career revolved around lawful access. It really did. We heard that the opposition delayed it. I will say that I do not know that the government made the best case for the bill. I think there were a lot of areas we really needed to address, but at the end of the day, crime is not an issue.

What I want to see is the best bill possible and, as parliamentarians, we should be endeavouring for the best bill possible. When people say we need speedy passage, no, we need proper passage and we need prudent passage. I will always scrutinize bills to get prudent bills.
Mr. Speaker, first off, I want to offer my condolences to the family and friends of the individual mentioned by my hon. colleague.
I would like to know if he looked at comparable provisions enacted in other countries, like European nations and Australia.
If so, are there any aspects that we should keep in mind during our study of Bill C‑34, based on what is being done elsewhere?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question.

I am not an expert on what other jurisdictions are doing. In one jurisdiction, as I was preparing for the speech, I came across something, I believe it may have been in Australia, that said that, once the law was enacted, not necessarily every account disappeared for a young person. I think that is something we have to contend with.

The other thing we have to contend with, even with age verification, is that AI might be smart, it might be “intelligent”, but can it really differentiate between somebody that is 15, 16, 17 or 14? To me, those are the types of things we need to study a committee. We just heard about Bill C-22. I would invite the government not to rush through this. Let us hear from people from Australia, New Zealand and places like that, because it is important that we, as parliamentarians, hear everything on this bill.

Mr. Speaker, in the charter statement for this bill, the Department of Justice acknowledges that the bill engages freedom of expression under subsection 2(b) and equality rights under section 15, because it distinguishes on the basis of age, and, of course, privacy interests under section 8 because of the age verification.

I find it striking that the charter statement relies on future commission guidelines, future regulations and a number of things that have not been determined yet. I am just wondering if the member could comment on the work that needs to be done in committee to reassure Canadians in this way.
Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague has been a wonderful addition to our B.C. caucus and our federal caucus here in the 45th Parliament.

I have read a number of charter statements, and I am not always impressed. I would say that sometimes they are deficient. When we start talking about how the charter applies to things that no longer exist, I think that jeopardizes what the rule of law says should be unparalleled transparency. If we do not know what might be there in regulation, how can we say how the charter is going to apply?

Mr. Speaker, it is always a pleasure to rise in the House. Today, I will be speaking about Bill C-34, but before I begin, I want to take a moment to honour the memory of Chief Warrant Officer Ron Nutt, from my riding, who served in the 1st Hussars for over 30 years and sadly passed away at age 67. Taken too soon, he was a quiet, gentle man, but a really intelligent, forceful human being. He will be sorely missed.

When it comes to Bill C-34, I can tell members that I have been in Parliament for quite some time, and this is the third version we have seen of the bill. I am really happy. The first two were terrible, but this one is much better. My colleague, the member for Calgary Nose Hill, tabled a private member's bill on this topic, because I think we all agree that we need to protect children from online harms. That private member's bill, Bill C-216, informed a lot of the work of this one, which is definitely helpful.

What the bill would do is make what is illegal today in the real world illegal in the digital world. That is a simplification, but it is essentially what is happening. We really need to protect our children and ourselves because the rise in online harm has been unbelievable. In 2023, half of students were experiencing online bullying. In 2024, police reported 19,516 instances of online child exploitation, an increase of 59% over the previous year and an increase of 500% since 2014. In terms of harms, we see that they are not just online. They are becoming physical and mental harms.

I am still struck and saddened by what happened to Amanda Todd and Rehtaeh Parsons. We studied this the first year I was elected. These girls had, without their consent, intimate images of them put up on Facebook, and as a result, they both took their own lives. It is just terrible. This is where online harm can become physical harm.

We also see the impact on our children. The pandemic was a time when many people spent more time online and could not go outside. Young people's depression doubled. Their anxiety quadrupled. The suicide rate among young people doubled as well. Online harms are a real deal for our kids, and we all want to protect our kids.

Each parliamentarian in the House has probably experienced online vitriol aimed at them. Certainly I have. It was awful when I started, but I have seen nothing like what I saw in the last year. These are harms. These things are illegal, and we have to address them.

When it comes to online harm, people will ask what it really is. The things that are defined in the bill include content that sexually victimizes a child or revictimizes a survivor, intimate content communicated without consent, content that induces a child to harm themselves, content used to bully a child, content that foments extreme hatred, content that incites violence, and terrorism or violent extremism content. Essentially, those things would be covered.

There have been concerns expressed about the freedom of expression and some of the charter rights. Everyone will know that I am a passionate defender of our Charter of Rights and Freedoms, and certainly the government is well aware that people are concerned about who is going to determine what can be said and what cannot be said. We have a good definition of hate speech, which has been recently improved, but we need to make sure that everything is clear and that we not have overreach happen. In terms of privacy, I have also heard the concerns there. Bill C-36 would address many of the concerns that I have heard raised in debate today.

In addition to that, people have talked about the need for transparency. I want to be clear about the digital commission that would be put in place. Obviously, if we are going to try to do something about online harms, we need somebody whose job it is to respond when bad behaviour is pointed out and come up with a remedy. That is why we want to take the idea from Bill C-216 to put the onus on service providers to make sure they are enforcing the standards. However, this digital commission, which would have three to five experts in the area, would be responsible for enforcing the laws that are described, and every year it would report to the minister and produce a report that would be tabled here in Parliament. Then Parliament could have oversight to make sure that it is working, that there are no abuses and that we are comfortable with where it is headed.

There have also been discussions about under-16 age verification. Different techniques can be used, and I look forward to the discussions at committee reviewing what other countries have done and reviewing what people think is a better method to ensure age verification. There is everything from uploading an ID, which some people think is a privacy violation, to using AI to guess how old someone is. That is getting very accurate, but I do not want it to guess how old I am, so I will stop there.

The other thing we have to do is be realistic. We know that when Australia implemented this, 70% of kids under 16 found a way around the system, so this will probably happen. It is important to say what is bad behaviour, say it is illegal and put mechanisms in place to enforce the rule of law, but we will have to deal with how we as parents and legislators encourage kids not to expose themselves at a young age to what is really the wild west of the Internet, where content that they should not be seeing is showing up. We know it is harmful to them.

I think about when I grew up. I did not even have a TV until I was eight. I never had a cellphone until I was 30. There would be some advantage to not having the social harms that kids have to deal with when their maturity and the confidence they have in themselves are not yet developed.

Let us talk a bit about what the safety commission would do. It would review the safety plans that are prepared and published for the different social media AI chatbot services. It would evaluate whether the age verification mechanism that the services are using is adequate. It would maintain transparency from both social media and chatbot platforms in publishing their policies and thresholds for notifying the RCMP, police or other law enforcement. Let us keep in mind that what is illegal in the real world would be illegal digitally, but the people who would follow up on that would not be in the digital safety commission; they would be the police of jurisdiction in that area. The commission would also provide support for victims of online harms and users of online services, and it would have the ability to issue fines to platforms of up to 3% of their global revenue.

I have a lot of respect for the member for Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola. He has encouraged the government to consider more serious sentencing, especially in cases of child luring and sexual exploitation. I think the government should take that into consideration.

There are some potential myths we have heard about this bill because of some of the previous versions that were not great. Let me just quickly look to those. One is that the government would get access to our private data. That would be specifically excluded; that would not happen. I already talked about the freedom of speech and already talked about the other concerns. I have also heard from the Bloc the concern that this bill would violate provincial jurisdiction. I look forward to hearing those discussions at committee. They have implemented something with age 14, so the discussion of what age it should be is a very good discussion.
With that, I would be happy to answer any questions.

Mr. Speaker, right at the beginning, the member said that this is a better bill, and I think when it comes to children, we need the best. Under the seven categories of harmful content, Bill C-34 lists “content used to bully a child”. There is currently no legal definition of bullying. I would like to ask the member if she can define what bullying is and provide an example.

Mr. Speaker, I am not a lawyer, so I highly recommend having a discussion with the member for Kamloops—Thompson—Nicola because he will know the answer to that, but I believe there is a bullying definition used in the law.

I would reiterate that some of the types of bullying we see use sexual images, for example, as in the Amanda Todd and Rehtaeh Parsons examples. I would point the member to the Twitter feed about me this past year if he wants to see what bullying looks like.
Mr. Speaker, I want congratulate my hon. colleague on her speech. It was very substantive. Of course, I am sorry that she had to endure so much harassment on social media. That is truly unacceptable.

At the end of her speech, she touched on several of the concerns that have been raised during this debate, including respect for areas of provincial jurisdiction, respect for Quebec and the provinces and, for example, flexibility regarding age.

In her view, does the bill, in its current form, provide sufficient flexibility? If, as she said, amendments were proposed during the committee study, would her party be open to improving the bill in this regard?
Mr. Speaker, I am not sufficiently familiar with the situation in Quebec.
I believe that Quebec has more experience with this issue, and I would be very pleased to see amendments tabled in committee.
Mr. Speaker, I first want to commend my colleague from Sarnia—Lambton—Bkejwanong for her outstanding work.
I was honestly quite touched to hear her talk about her experience. She has been very courageous in all of this. I am very pleased to have her on our team. As I said, she is doing a great job.

That said, she mentioned at the beginning of her speech that there were other versions of this legislation that were not as good as this one. I would like her to tell us about the main ways in which this bill improves on them and what she likes most about this version of this very important bill.
Mr. Speaker, there was something unacceptable in the previous versions.

The first two versions said that if somebody thought a person was going to commit a hate crime in the future, that person could be put in prison for up to 25 years. That seemed, to me, very much like the movie Minority Report. It is certainly not charter-compliant, so I am glad to see that it was removed.

Mr. Speaker, I respect enormously the fact that the member is an engineer. I am a lawyer. I look at this bill and ask why we do not tighten it to create a real incentive for tech giants to live up to the duty to protect our children, enforceable by law. By attaching that duty specifically to the directors of the companies, they would feel a real incentive to avoid ending up with strict liability and going to jail if a child in Canada is harmed.

I want to put forward amendments to that effect when we get to committee. I will vote for the bill to get to committee. We need to tackle this. I wonder if she has any thoughts on the idea of tightening up the punishments.

Mr. Speaker, as an engineer, I am very detail-oriented in general. I would say the more detail we can put in the bill and not leave to regulators or bureaucrats, the better. I look forward to the amendments the member opposite will bring to committee.

Mr. Speaker, I am truly grateful for this opportunity to speak to a topic that matters so much to me and to our fellow citizens. The digital safety act is not a response to some naive or made-up concern, nor are the proposals within it based on wishful thinking. It addresses a need that Canadians have been telling us about for some time. The whole world must contend with new realities, and it is time for our country to evolve and adapt to those realities. There is no doubt these challenges will keep getting bigger as technology evolves and as the people we represent require protection from new threats.
Let us wait no longer. Let us show that Canada knows how to evolve with the times. Let us also demonstrate, once again, what Canada is made of: We act for the good of all, including our young people.

Other G7 countries have passed legislation in response to this threat targeting our young people. For example, Australia has already enacted legislation raising the minimum age for social media access to 16. Here in this country, all Canadians, including parents and guardians, expect us to take action too.

Just as concerns about teenagers' access to social media platforms are well founded, the age proposed to allow them to access these platforms is also not random. It has been shown that the digital landscape is not safe for children under 16. For these children, the scales are more likely to tip towards harms than benefits. Setting a limit for children under 16 is consistent with scientific research, as well as with what other jurisdictions around the world have done.
Let me share some statistics.

In 2023, Canadian police recorded 19,516 incidents of online child sexual exploitation over the course of the year. Again, there were 19,516 incidents of online child sexual exploitation over a 12‑month period in our country. That amounts to more than two cases per hour, every hour, over one year. That is unacceptable and alarming. This was a 59% increase over the previous year and a 500% increase over just a few years. We can therefore conclude that the longer we wait before taking real and effective action to put an end to this type of appalling behaviour, the more it will increase exponentially.

We must work together to address this threat, because there is still time. Bill C-34 is not a quick fix or a band-aid solution. Bill C‑34 is not just about demonstrating that we are fulfilling our duty to protect Canada's young people. It is supported by many expert organizations, including the Children's Hospital of Eastern Ontario, the Hospital for Sick Children in Toronto, the Canadian Paediatric Society, Kids Help Phone and the youth advocacy sector. I would also note that the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child encourages the protection of young people from information or material that is injurious to their well-being. Bill C‑34 will ensure that we are in compliance with international ethical standards.

I would like to come back to some statistics. While social media cannot be blamed for everything, it is clear that its impact extends beyond physical safety of our kids, because it also has an impact on their mental health. Rates of depression, anxiety and suicidal ideation have risen exponentially among young Canadians over the past year. I would like to reiterate some of the figures my colleagues have already highlighted. Among Canadians aged 15 to 24, rates of depression have doubled, while rates of anxiety have quadrupled. Without a robust bill such as Bill C-34, these statistics will continue to rise. These statistics represent the next generation of Canadians and the impact this has on their individual life paths.

I do not have enough time today to provide all the statistics on this subject. For example, I did not mention that one in four young people between the ages of 12 and 17 in this country report having been cyber-bullied. One in four is a lot. We cannot allow this situation to keep getting worse. Instead, we should help young people experience this brief period of their lives in safety, as most of us had the opportunity to do, without being exposed to the same level of harm they face today. At the very least, the far more limited exposure many of us experienced likely spared us some of the dangers and mental health challenges. Now is the time to step up and demonstrate that we care about our children.

I would also like to acknowledge my riding's efforts in this regard. Sherbrooke is at the forefront of efforts to protect young people online. One notable local initiative was spearheaded by a group of law students at the Université de Sherbrooke. Last spring, they drafted a bill to address the harmful effects of excessive screen time on young people. Among other things, the bill would ban access to Facebook, X, Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat for those under 16. During a visit to the legislative buildings in Quebec City, the students said that they specifically targeted these apps because they are addictive. They also drew parallels with the arguments that led to the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco for minors.

Mr. Speaker, as we approach November 5, when our government will table budget 2026, I want to highlight what we have achieved through our previous budget. We removed the consumer carbon tax, introduced a GST rebate for first-time homebuyers, cut taxes for the middle class, made the national school food program permanent, hired 1,000 CBSA and 1,000 RCMP officers, introduced the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, provided $25 billion in support for workers impacted by tariffs and invested $1.2 billion to protect our oceans.

A coalition of 19 Filipino Canadian organizations from every province recently submitted the community's first unified pre-budget submission. As the member of Parliament for Hamilton Centre, which has a vibrant and integral Filipino community, I look forward to budget 2026 and the opportunities it will create for Filipino Canadians and all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, as Remembrance Day approaches, we honour those who sacrifice for our freedom. In the trenches, countless soldiers find hope and courage through their faith in God, yet the Liberal government has directed military chaplains to exclude references to God from prayers at public ceremonies. Faith in God has been a cornerstone of our country since Confederation, with roots in much older traditions. Our charter recognizes the supremacy of God. Our anthem declares, “God keep our land glorious and free”. How can we sing those words, yet bar chaplains from invoking God at our ceremonies?

Prayers comfort those who serve and those families who grieve. We must respect people of every faith and those of none. No one should be forced to pray, but there must be room for prayer. The Liberal government should respect the gratitude to God expressed by so many veterans and reverse—
The hon. member for Halifax.

Mr. Speaker, today I stand to recognize some of Canada's climate champions, this year's Clean50 honourees. Each year, the Clean50 awards celebrate Canada's sustainability heroes, recognizing the impact that individuals, community leaders, businesses and organizations have in addressing the climate crisis.

I am proud to be an alumni of this program. As we continue to experience the worsening impacts of climate change, it is more important than ever that we support our innovators and our trailblazers. Amazingly, over 10% of this year's Clean50 winners are based in Nova Scotia, some of whom I know well and have worked with.
I congratulate and welcome all of this year's honourees to the Clean50 family. Let us build our path to net zero together.
Mr. Speaker, as a former mayor myself, I want to congratulate those elected in Simcoe—Grey in this week's municipal elections.

In the town of Blue Mountains, there is Mayor Moreau, Deputy Mayor Gilliland and councillors McKinlay, Porter, Loney, Dewitt and McLeod. In Collingwood, there is Mayor Hamlin, Deputy Mayor Potts and councillors Ferrigan, MacCulloch, Perry, Baines, McCrimmon, McLeod and Ring. In Wasaga Beach, there is Mayor Smith, Deputy Mayor Foley and councillors Graves, Dileo, White, Timms and Belanger. In Clearview, there is Mayor McArthur, Deputy Mayor McGillvray and councillors Houghton, Walters, Broderick, Walker and Brooks. In Adjala-Tosorontio, there is Mayor Anderson, Deputy Mayor Lachs and councillors Mason, Cox, Reiber, Patterson and Gervasi. Finally, in Essa, there is Mayor Macdonald, Deputy Mayor Smith and councillors Maltby, Sander and Kiezebrink.
I want to say best wishes and a big thank you to everyone who shared their vision and put their name on the ballot.

Mr. Speaker, on October 14, I was pleased to join the Carleton District School Board and the Mulroney family for the official opening of the Brian Mulroney Elementary School in Orléans. This new English public school will welcome nearly 700 students, inspiring future generations to learn, lead and succeed.
As we mark Small Business Week, I also wanted to recognize the local small businesses that are the backbone of Orléans' economy, creating jobs, supporting families and strengthening our community.

Finally, Orléans has much to celebrate. Two outstanding residents were recently recognized for their contributions. Gipsy Ghosh received the 2026 Famous 5 Ottawa award, while Amanda Kilabuk received the Governor General’s Awards in Commemoration of the Persons Case. Their leadership and dedication inspire others and make our community proud.
Please join me in congratulating Gipsy and Amanda on these well-deserved honours.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to recognize Ellen Crothers, a wonderful volunteer in S, D and G, for her outstanding community leadership and heartfelt service. Ellen was recently named the recipient of the Community Service Award at South Glengarry's business and community awards gala. Through the Mathew Crothers memorial charity, founded in honour of her son, she has transformed personal loss into lasting support for local families. Her dedication embodies the spirit and community values recognized by the award.

Mathew's Toy Mountain has, for two decades, collected donations and gifts for children in need and supported patients at CHEO. We are looking forward to the upcoming gala on November 7 to support the charity's work. Mathew's legacy is certainly being carried on through this vital work by Ellen and a great network of local supporters and donors.
I offer congratulations and thanks to Ellen. Mathew would be so proud to know of all the work being done in his memory.
Mr. Speaker, last week, history was made on the Hill as we—
I know that sometimes the noise comes from outside the walls of the chamber, but I think now it is coming from inside the chamber.
I will let the hon. member start over.

Mr. Speaker, last week, history was made here at the House of Commons as we had the Filipino-Canadian Coalition, representing 19 national organizations from across Canada, from 10 provinces and one territory, come to talk about how to unlock the full potential and talent found within the Filipino community.

We know that the Filipino community has pushed so much to build this country economically and socially, and to build our cultural fabric. We are looking for ways to support it by building community infrastructure to unlock that talent. I will be working with the community to look for ways to build, and it wants to commit to building a stronger country, building Canada strong.
My thanks go to the Filipino-Canadian Coalition for all the work it is doing, bringing this network here to the House of Commons and building the Filipino community here in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Canadians received very bad news. The Bank of Canada has to raise the policy rate to 2.5%. That is the first increase in three years. This time, the Prime Minister cannot blame the old Liberal government.

In its report, the Bank of Canada indicates that grocery prices will increase more quickly in 2027 because of rising energy costs that are reverberating throughout the food supply chains. The bank also points out that rising diesel prices are driving up costs for farmers.
The Conservatives have been saying that for a while now. We have to develop our natural resources, eliminate federal fuel taxes to bring prices down, and give families a chance.
In practical terms, what do these increases mean for families? They mean higher mortgage payments, higher grocery prices, higher gas prices, and less money in families' pockets.
What is the Prime Minister, a former top banker, gearing up to do? He plans to spend, spend, spend, run deficits and add even more to the debt.
One thing is for sure: 11 years of Liberal rule has been quite costly.

Mr. Speaker, this morning, representatives of thousands of newspapers and magazines from both sides of the Atlantic wrote to Canada and the European Union. They are calling on them to use the upcoming summit as an opportunity to commit to regulating digital platforms and the use of AI. They are calling for the summit's final statement to include “a firm, shared commitment to free, independent, pluralistic and sustainable media and reliable professional journalism, underpinned by enabling frameworks.”

They also call on Canada and Europe to promote “a transparent AI ecosystem that respects intellectual property rights, supports licensing and appropriate remuneration, and enables creators, publishers and other cultural and creative businesses to control and realise the value of their works.”
Canadian and European media are highlighting the most significant global challenges for the future of culture and news. The Prime Minister must raise these issues at the Canada-EU summit today.
Mr. Speaker, I recognize an important Canadian naval heritage initiative marking the 25th anniversary of Operation Apollo and the events of September 11, 2001.

A new project mapping Canada's naval response to 9/11 in the Middle East, HMCS Vancouver's mission for Operation Apollo, will digitally preserve and share a critical chapter of our nation's military history. Supported by Veterans Affairs, this initiative is transforming historical ship logbooks into an interactive, web-based map documenting HMCS Vancouver's 79 days in the North Arabian Sea.

I would like to recognize Blue Horizon Geomatics and my constituent, Theresa Fingler, whose experience aboard HMCS Vancouver brings exceptional depth and authenticity to the project. This initiative honours our veterans and ensures that their service is never forgotten.

Mr. Speaker, we are heartbroken by the horrific bombing at St. George's Greek Orthodox Church in Jordan. Innocent lives were taken in a sacred moment of worship in a place that should have been a sanctuary. We grieve with the families of the people killed, and we pray for the wounded and for the community shaken to its core.

This attack is a painful reminder that the persecution of Christians is growing around the world. Freedom of worship is a fundamental human right, yet millions of believers, including here in Canada, still face violence, discrimination and fear simply for practising their faith.

Canada must stand firmly for religious freedom, demand justice for victims and work to protect vulnerable faith communities wherever they are threatened. Terror will not silence a prayer, and hatred will not extinguish faith.
Our prayers and unwavering solidarity remain with the victims, their families and persecuted Christians everywhere.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to condemn the horrific attack against Christians in the kingdom of Jordan that took place last Friday, when armed fanatics stormed a Greek Orthodox church and killed nine people and injured 40 during a funeral. They were killed only because they were Christians.
I appreciate and value the response and support of His Majesty King Abdullah II ibn Al Hussein and the Jordanian authorities.

All minorities have an inalienable right to safety and dignity under the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, whether they are Muslim, Jewish or Christian. This attack is an assault on humanity and on the idea of peaceful coexistence between communities.
I stand in solidarity with the people of Jordan as well as with all Christians in the Middle East.
May the victims rest in peace and may they live on forever in our memory.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's Bank of Canada interest rate adds to the gut-wrenching anxiety Canadians are feeling. Borrowing costs are going up right away for people with truck loans, variable rate mortgages and lines of credit. Those with fixed-rate mortgages facing renewal are wondering how big a hole this is going to blow in budgets that are already shot. The mountain that first-time homebuyers have to climb got steeper, while the costs of everything else keep going up. Higher costs are not going to do anything to help bring down the cost of rent.

The Bank of Canada says it acted because of high inflation. Well, the people of Nanaimo—Ladysmith will be watching the budget closely to see whether the government finally stops its inflationary spending. People are sick of having to put off necessary repairs, delay investments and put their lives on hold. We expect to see a credible plan to bring down the cost of food and gas and to make housing more attainable for our youth, not more announcements and promises that do not—
The hon member for Saint-Léonard—Saint-Michel.

Mr. Speaker, as the chair of the Canadian Section of ParlAmericas, I am delighted to welcome here today in Ottawa a delegation of members of Mexico's chamber of deputies. ParlAmericas brings legislators from across the Americas and the Caribbean together to strengthen parliamentary dialogue and democratic governance and to build lasting partnerships.

Today's visits builds on the Canadian Section of ParlAmericas delegation's bilateral visit to Mexico last March, ahead of the joint review of CUSMA, where I had the honour of meeting and engaging with members of parliament from Mexico. That visit provided a timely opportunity to let our Mexican counterparts know the importance of maintaining strong Canada-Mexico co-operation as we look to the future of North American trade and economic integration.
Their presence here today is a testament to the strong bonds that exist between Canada and Mexico and to our shared commitment to democracy, dialogue and co-operation.

ParaText.I: Bienvenida a toda la delegación mexicana en Canadá.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Bank of Canada raised interest rates to 2.5%, the first hike since July 2023, adding more pressure on Canadian families. The bank's own press release warned of “the risk that continuing high energy prices spread broadly to the prices of other goods and services.” Governor Macklem also warned that further increases may be necessary.

Canada is blessed with abundant energy resources. Our policies should reflect that advantage, not undermine it. Monetary policy cannot carry the burden of economic stability alone. As government spending increases, fiscal discipline and affordable energy must be central to the government's policy, not casualties of it.

The Prime Minister once understood price stability from the governor's chair. It is now time to demonstrate that same understanding from the Prime Minister's Office, exercise fiscal restraints and eliminate the industrial carbon tax.
Mr. Speaker, today I am very pleased to welcome the students of École secondaire Saint‑Maxime, which is in my riding of Vimy, in Laval.

By visiting Parliament, they are getting a wonderful opportunity to learn about the institutions that shape our country and the democratic values that unite us and make our nation free, welcoming and among the most prosperous in the world. Visiting Parliament is the best way for anyone, especially a young person, to truly understand how our representative democracy works.

I want to express my gratitude to the staff of École secondaire Saint‑Maxime for their dedication to these young people. I also want to thank all those who contribute to their future success and their growth as responsible citizens. In Canada, everyone can find a place to belong, make their voice heard and achieve their dreams while playing an active role in civic life.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, while Canadians can no longer afford food or housing, the Prime Minister tried to divert their attention with his grand plan to become an associate member of the European Union. No one knows what that means, and the Europeans rejected it yesterday. We already have a free trade agreement with Europe, but nine countries have not ratified it.
Does the Prime Minister promise to get them to ratify the agreement, or is this summit just for show?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we are delighted to have the Prime Minister, as well as many of my colleagues, in Montreal today for our annual meeting with European Union leaders. We will explore a wide range of opportunities for collaboration beyond the free trade agreement we have already negotiated.
Canada needs to diversify its markets, and that is exactly what we are doing.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has tried to distract Canadians from crazy housing and food costs for the last two months with his big project of Canada becoming an associate member of the EU. Nobody knows what it means and the Europeans have now rejected it. We already have a free trade agreement with Europe. It is just that nine of its countries refuse to ratify that agreement.

Will the Prime Minister actually get anything real done at this big grand summit, get those countries to ratify the deal, let in our beef or is this just another Seinfeld summit, a meeting about nothing?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if anyone would know anything about Seinfeld, it is that leader who wakes up every day and lives the same recurring nightmare, every single day.

The Prime Minister and my colleagues are in Montreal for the annual Canada-EU Summit. This year we are exploring many areas of further co-operation beyond the free trade arrangements we have with Europe. We are going to diversify our markets, we going to diversify them away from the United States, and that is good news for Canada.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is actually a recurring nightmare for the Canadian people who cannot afford to pay their grocery bills and whose mortgage payments just went up yesterday because of deficit spending by the government. The Prime Minister acts like George Costanza, running around the office trying to look busy while achieving nothing at all in the real world.

Let us look at this. Nine countries have not ratified the EU free trade agreement. Will he get them to ratify? They are still blocking our beef. Will he remove those blockages? They are threatening an industrial carbon tariff. Will he have that removed, or will it just be about nothing?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this guy talks like Kramer. He just walks into the room and, every time, says something weird.

More seriously, free trade with Europe is a great thing for Canada. More collaboration with Europe on defence and procurement, and making sure that Canadians and Canadian youth can study and research, and we can co-operate on things like AI.
Yes, his least favourite topic will be co-operating on democracy. I want to thank the Leader of the Opposition. It is going to be great.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, everybody loves Kramer.

If he wants to talk about something weird, the Prime Minister told us that if we brought in a big industrial carbon tax on our steel, aluminum, cement and concrete, the Europeans would let our industrial goods in tariff-free. It turns out they are now threatening a carbon tariff on Canada, at the same time the Prime Minister holds his grand summit.

He has already failed to get American tariffs lifted, like he promised in the election. Can Prime Minister tell us, is he going to stand up to the Europeans and make sure there is no carbon tariff on our goods?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, among the many areas of co-operation with Europe that we will obviously be discussing today and will be discussing going forward, in terms of our much closer arrangement with the European Union, will indeed be energy.

I noted with great pleasure that my colleague, the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources saluted the fact that the first gas shipments going to Germany left the West Coast in these past months, and we can expect much more energy co-operation with our friends in the European Union.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has told Canadians for the last two years to ignore their grocery bills, their rising gas prices and the fact that an entire generation cannot afford a place to live because he has got these grand signing ceremonies of meaningless documents. Here we are, with no commitment from the nine European holdouts to sign on and ratify the existing free trade agreement we have or to allow our beef in or to cancel their planned carbon tariff.
Why is the Prime Minister not delivering real results? Is it because this is just another public relations stunt?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have a free trade arrangement with Europe. It is in effect right now. I have even better news. The Prime Minister has set an ambitious objective for Canada to double our non-U.S. exports. I want to tell the leader the news is in: We are on track and beyond to doubling our non-U.S. exports over the next 10 years. We will do it by investing in our ports. We will do it by investing in projects, in energy and especially in our people by building Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have to admire the hubris of a party whose members stands up over there and brag about promises that they have made that they have not kept. They are going to a summit with a continent that already has a free trade agreement, but nine of its members have not signed on to it. They will not commit to getting a single one of those countries to sign. In fact, not one of their leaders will be there. Then they are blocking our beef and pork, and the Liberals will not commit to getting that removed at this summit.
Speaking of beef and pork, is this not just another big nothing burger?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think Canadians look, with a great deal of pride, at the events in Montreal today, where our Prime Minister is going to break new trails in terms of co-operation with the European Union, and with new arrangements in AI, in democracy, in transportation and in trade. These are all areas where we can more closely collaborate with our European friends, diversify our markets, build Canada strong, and make sure that Canada works with like-minded nations to keep our people prosperous and keep our people working.
Mr. Speaker, Quebec wants to boost trade with Europe in the face of the tariff crisis, but CBC is reporting that Canada is going to hamper our efforts.

The European Union imposes tariffs on products from countries with poor environmental records. Since Canada, unlike Quebec, has scrapped its carbon pricing, it is exposing us to penalties. An internal memo estimates that $2.8 billion worth of goods will be subject to tariffs next year, including $800 million on aluminum, steel and iron from Quebec alone.
Do the Liberals realize that their climate capitulation is standing in the way of Quebec trade?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Bloc Québécois is peddling all sorts of falsehoods.
First, we are working with the European Union on a wide range of collaborative projects, whether in the fields of artificial intelligence, democracy or closer co-operation in a number of areas.

We are also working with the European Union because it needs energy. I was particularly interested to hear my colleague, the Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, announce that the first shipments of LNG have left Canada's west coast.
Mr. Speaker, the CBC must appreciate the minister's disregard for it.

For years, the Bloc Québécois has been warning the federal government that Quebec will be hit harder by European tariffs if Canada ends its carbon pricing. Well, that time has come. Even if Quebec maintains its carbon pricing, 800 million dollars' worth of our Quebec metals will still be subject to tariffs. Thanks to Canada, we are going to face more customs barriers.
Are the Liberals proud of the harm they are doing to Quebec's exports?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Quebec's aluminum is one of the greenest in the world. Our government has attracted new investments and collaborations with Canadian aluminum producers, and we are not stopping there.

To be very clear: If the Bloc Québécois is interested in reducing greenhouse gases, all it has to do is support the biggest greenhouse gas reduction project of all: the high-speed rail project connecting cities in Quebec to cities Ontario.
Mr. Speaker, Europe is going to impose tariffs on Quebec's aluminum, steel and iron exports because of Canada.

This may not end with metal exports, because the Liberals also weakened pesticide regulations and even gave themselves the power to reintroduce banned pesticides. Europe has strict standards in this area as well, so that will hinder agri-food trade. Unlike the Liberals, Europe takes these issues seriously.
Do they now realize how much their irresponsible deregulation will cost Quebec?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Europe is throwing open its doors to co-operation with Canada. It was a historic day, during which we explored a wide range of opportunities to deepen our co-operation with France, Romania, Spain and Germany. We will continue to strengthen these relationships across a number of sectors, expanding access to European markets for Canadian companies and individuals, including Quebeckers, who stand to benefit greatly.

Mr. Speaker, today the Auditor General released a sobering report on Canada's anti-money laundering watchdog, FINTRAC, which reports directly to the Minister of Finance. Here is the bottom line up front. The AG said, “FINTRAC did not effectively carry out its role in overseeing compliance with Canada's anti-money laundering laws” and that “limited FINTRAC's ability to help detect, prevent, and deter money laundering.”
Does the Minister of Finance accept the Auditor General's findings that his agency is failing to prevent money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion in Canada?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our government is committed to protecting the integrity of Canada's financial system and supporting the institutions that safeguard it. We are taking concrete steps to develop a national anti-fraud strategy in collaboration with industry partners and agencies. We are also creating the financial crimes agency, which will lead the fight against sophisticated financial crimes with increased RCMP resources. If the Conservatives are concerned about combatting money laundering, we encourage them to support Bill C-29.

Mr. Speaker, if the government was serious about this issue, it would have created the agency, which it promised in 2021, and it would not have missed the legal deadline to review the Proceeds of Crime, Money Laundering, and Terrorist Financing Act.

The reality is that police need timely access to this information, and yet the Auditor General found that it took on average 112 days for FINTRAC to give law enforcement information, and said that it was, “too late to be useful.”
Why is the Minister of Finance not giving police across Canada the tools and information they need to stop money laundering and terrorist financing?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, again, our government is committed to protecting and safeguarding the integrity of Canada's financial system. We have taken concrete steps to develop an anti-fraud strategy in collaboration with many partners. We are in the process of creating the financial crimes agency that will lead the fight against ever more sophisticated financial crimes. We have given the RCMP additional resources to help coordinate these efforts. If the Conservatives are concerned about this issue, they should support our bill, Bill C-29.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada says inflation is rising and economic growth is slowing, while the Parliamentary Budget Officer says interest on the national debt is the fastest-growing government expense. The cost of government is driving up the cost of living and these Liberals have broken every fiscal promise, smashed through every fiscal guardrail and cut loose every fiscal anchor they have ever set. For 11 straight years, they have tabled deficits.
When will the government finally stop its inflationary deficit spending?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, unlike the Conservatives, we believe in the independence of monetary policy in our central bank, and we know that inflation is being driven by the war in the Middle East.

Unlike the Conservatives, we are stepping up every single day in this House to offer more affordability supports for Canadians when they need it most. We have cut taxes on income, housing, fuel and new business investment. We have enhanced and increased access to federal benefits, like the groceries and essentials benefit, and we are investing to create tens of thousands of new jobs all across Canada. That is how we build Canada strong. That is how we support Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, unemployment is up, grocery costs are up, inflation is up and now interest rates are up. Yesterday, deficit-fuelled inflation caused the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates, with the six big banks following. For those who own a home, their mortgage payment just got more expensive, and for those aspiring to buy one, that dream has just been pushed further out of reach, all because the Prime Minister could not control his spending.
With their upcoming budget, will the Liberals stop their inflationary spending?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Buckley Belanger (Secretary of State (Rural Development), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the Conservative caucus members from Saskatchewan awaken from their slumber, this is what has been happening in Saskatchewan.

Since June alone, I have been part of federal announcements representing a more than $467-million investment in Saskatchewan, and canola sales are increasing. We have spent money in support of child care, and canola sales are improving. We have spent money in community infrastructure, and canola sales are improving. We have spent money in indigenous communities, and canola sales are improving.
I think maybe the member and the entire Saskatchewan—
The hon. member for Louis‑Saint‑Laurent—Akiawenhrahk.

Mr. Speaker, this is terrible news for all Canadian families. Yesterday, the Bank of Canada announced that, for the first time in three years, the key interest rate is set to rise and inflation is set to climb to 3.5% for the year as a whole.

What does this mean in practical terms? It means that mortgage rates will rise. It risks slowing home sales, placing additional pressure on homeowners and bringing housing construction to a standstill.
Is there a single minister in this government who actually understands that colossal debts and deficits lead to inflation?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if the member opposite had been paying attention to what the government has been doing for almost a year and a half now, he would see that we have been focusing on affordability. We lowered taxes for 22 million Canadians. We introduced the Canada groceries and essentials benefit.

However, there is something that I still do not understand and that is why I am asking him this question: Given the cost of living, why did he vote against the Canada child benefit, which provides $79 million for 22,845 children in his riding of Louis-Saint-Laurent—Akiawenhrahk? That is approximately $3,500 per child in his riding, and his riding is home to nearly 23,000 children.
Why did he vote against that?

Mr. Speaker, I would invite the minister to update his statistics or, at the very least, check with the the Governor of the Bank of Canada to get the latest figures. The governor is the one saying that the Liberals' management of the economy is a complete mess. What is the result? Grocery prices are going to go up. The governor is saying that prices will rise faster than last year, and things were already terrible last year. That is what life is like after 11 years of Liberal governance.
Can the minister tell Canadians or the Governor of the Bank of Canada why the Liberals' inflationary policies are causing grocery prices to rise even more sharply this year than last year?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, let us be clear about Canada's fiscal position. Canada is one of only two G7 countries with a AAA rating. We have a better debt-to-GDP ratio and deficit-to-GDP ratio than our G7 peers.

However, what I still do not understand is why the member insists on systematically voting against measures that have a very direct impact, whether it is a tax cut, the groceries and essentials benefit or the Canadian dental care plan. Those programs affect 23,614 residents in his riding, not to mention the 23,000 children who are benefiting from the Canada child benefit.
If he wants to talk about helping families, he should put his vote where his mouth is.

Mr. Speaker, Breakfast Club of Canada told committee this week that the $1-billion school food program has lost 22% of its grocery purchasing power because of inflation, yet the minister keeps insisting that the program feeds an extra 400,000 kids a year. The math does not math. When we divide the money over five years and 180 school days per year, it averages less than three dollars per target child per day, but a five-province study found that the average lunch costs $6.45, double, which feeds a lot fewer kids.
Will the minister table the national data and costing behind her claims? Hungry kids want to check her homework.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we absolutely take no lessons from the other side of the House when it comes to the national school food program. I was at that committee meeting, and I heard from the Coalition for Healthy School Food, from the Breakfast Club of Canada and from students who have written to our Prime Minister about how the national school food program is helping them every single day in their schools. The member should listen up.

Mr. Speaker, no one should be surprised to see the Premier of Quebec asserting his role on the international stage. Yesterday, I asked the most senior officials at Global Affairs Canada whether they were familiar with the Gérin-Lajoie doctrine. Not one of them could tell me what it was. It has been the cornerstone of Quebec's international relations policy for over 60 years, yet Ottawa has never heard of it.
How is it possible that the federal bureaucracy has become so out of touch with Quebec?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mona Fortier (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as the Prime Minister said, Quebec is a distinct nation that flourishes within a strong Canada.

In an increasingly dangerous and divided world, we must be masters in our own home and build reliable partnerships for Canadians. We recognize Quebec's unique economic and cultural interests, and we will continue to work with its government, particularly in areas such as education, culture and the francophone community.
The Canadian economy is stronger when we work together.

Mr. Speaker, for over 60 years, Quebec has conducted its own international relations in areas under its jurisdiction. It has been doing so for more than 60 years. However, it is clear that Canada does not respect Quebec's prerogatives, as illustrated by Canada's refusal to let Mr. St-Pierre Plamondon speak at the Canada-European Union summit. That is not even the worst of it.
The federal government is no longer even aware of Quebec's prerogatives. This strikes me as the ultimate proof that Canada does not understand our nation and cannot speak for us. Is that not true?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mona Fortier (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the provinces and territories bring valuable expertise to Canada's international relationships.

The fact that Montreal is hosting the Canada-European Union summit reflects Quebec's important role in strengthening this partnership. We have always worked closely with the provinces and territories, and we will continue to do so to diversify our relationships abroad. We are focused on delivering real results for Canadians across the country.

Mr. Speaker, in Kelowna, a man violently chokes his wife. He is arrested. He is released on bail. Thirty minutes later, he shows up again. He assaults her again. He chokes her again. He is arrested again. Under the Liberal laws, guess what: He is released on bail again. The Liberals promised they would fix the broken bail system, but nothing has changed. Under their watch, intimate partner violence is up 40%.
How many times must a woman be attacked before the Liberals put her safety first?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, because we are so concerned about incidents such as this, we put forward the Protecting Victims Act in Bill C-16, and we put forward the bail reform legislation. It all passed in June. Those laws have been implemented starting July 15, but it is the job of the provinces to make sure they are applying these pieces of legislation. The changes have gone into effect in the code. It is time for the provinces to catch up.

Mr. Speaker, the criminals are laughing at the Liberal justice system, and the victims are the ones paying the price. A guy with 274 convictions gets bail. Convicted child killers and rapists are attending cooking classes and law school. McDonald's, booze, drugs and illegal guns are being delivered by drones into our maximum-security prisons. It sounds insane but that is the sad reality under the Liberal government.
Will the Liberals put the criminals behind bars and stop putting Canadian lives at risk?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the federal government is responsible for the Criminal Code of Canada. We have made an unprecedented number of changes to stiffen our laws, to make sure criminals will serve longer sentences and so repeat offenders do not get bail, but it is the job of the provinces to apply these new changes. I hope the provinces will catch up.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals constantly boast about how they fixed bail in their eyes. We as Conservatives warned them that they did not go far enough.

Recently in Kelowna, a man was accused of assaulting and choking his intimate partner. He was released on bail. Within 30 minutes, he is alleged to have been back at her house, again choking her, and now breaching a no-contact order. He was again released on bail.
People expect the government to protect the most vulnerable. Will the Liberals admit that their bail changes did not go far enough, and commit to acting?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if my hon. colleague had actually read the legislation that we put forward, he would know that, on the advice of the provincial government in British Columbia, we added specific provisions to address cases of intimate partner violence that involve strangulation, because we know and accept that it is predictive of future violence. When we adapt these laws, we expect provinces to put them into action by appropriately resourcing the system and those who are appointed to make decisions to put these rules into force.
Tragic circumstances such as these can motivate change. We have taken action, and we are looking forward to seeing the changes implemented by the people within positions—

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice asked whether I bothered to read his bill. Did he bother to read my bill on the intimate partner violence that happened to Bailey McCourt? I will let the House know that this offence occurred in Kelowna. Do members know what else occurred in Kelowna? The murder of Bailey McCourt, who was killed three hours after her abuser left the courthouse after conviction.
It is our job as parliamentarians to protect the most vulnerable. The Liberals should have passed our jail not bail act, which was exponentially harder on bail.
Will the Liberals admit they have a problem on their hands and they need to fix it now?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Sean Fraser (Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada and Minister responsible for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the member questions whether I read his bill. He should know very well that I have, because we worked together across partisan lines to rewrite that bill. He should know that we worked together with family members in the tragic circumstances of Bailey McCourt's murder to ensure that she did not die in vain, and to change the law in this country to protect future victims of intimate partner violence and murder against harms we know are preventable.
I appreciated the member's non-partisan spirit of collaboration. It is a shame that it seems to have come to an end.

Mr. Speaker, there was heartbreaking news out of Toronto this morning. Three masked suspects armed with handguns and a hammer forced their way into a family's home, and a father and his two daughters were shot. This is the kind of chaos that Canadians are facing. It is time for the Liberals to pass our stand on guard act and our safe at home bill that would strengthen protections for Canadians by strengthening our self-defence laws and ensuring that we have laws on the books that protect families in their own home.
Will the Liberals pass these laws so we can protect Canadians and restore safe homes, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):
