Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the incident referenced by the member is a very tragic news story that I learned about today as well. I hear that the Toronto Police Service has an ongoing investigation. We are waiting for the investigation's findings.

Of course, we are adamant about making sure that criminals who enter anyone's home are caught and appropriately sentenced. That is why we have made an unprecedented number of changes to the Criminal Code of Canada. It is the job of local police and the local courts that are provincially run to now—
The hon. member for Oakville West.

Mr. Speaker, the work our government is doing to diversify Canadian trade matters for the workers in my riding of Oakville West, who produce top-quality products that are in demand around the world. The recently concluded Canada-U.A.E. trade agreement marks a historic milestone for our country to expand trade ties with our largest trading partner in the Middle East.

Could the Minister of International Trade update the House on how our record-setting U.A.E. trade agreement will help Canadian businesses across the country tap into this fast-growing market and ensure that Canadian workers and exporters compete and win on the world stage?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Maninder Sidhu (Minister of International Trade, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, through you, I would like to thank my colleague from Oakville West for her work in the House and, of course, on the trade committee.

This week, we signed a historic trade agreement with the U.A.E. in a record 47 days, the fastest trade agreement ever negotiated by Canada. Once in force, this new trade agreement will lower tariffs on 99% of Canada's exports to the U.A.E. That means new opportunities for Canadian workers and businesses and a market value of over $700 billion. That is more access for Canadian agriculture, aerospace, energy, lumber and more.
Plan A is working. We are diversifying and are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, recent data shows that we have an innovation exodus to the United States. It is up 142%. Thirty-four per cent of immigrants with a Ph.D. leave Canada within 25 years, and the innovation sector earns 46% more in the United States.

The Liberals have brought in too many people too fast for housing and health care, and now Canada's best and brightest are leaving, including those who bring real innovation and jobs to our economy. Why is the Prime Minister not trying to reverse this brain drain instead of planning for higher immigration levels?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, innovation and research are very important priorities for our government.

Budget 2025 launched an international talent attraction strategy and action plan. This will support recruitment of world-class researchers and advance Canada's global competitiveness and research excellence.

What we have also seen in the last six to nine months is that a large number of U.S.-based, top-notch researchers have come to Canada, including to Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, and this will accelerate—
The hon. member for Niagara South.

Mr. Speaker, on the contrary, we are sitting in an immigration system that has over 30,000 people who want to come to Canada under the start-up visa program and are stuck in bureaucratic purgatory. That is not progress. That is a failure of our system.

On the flip side, today's national security strategy is a nothingburger and fails to address the serious screening problems for non-citizens seeking entry to Canada. The CBSA had 675 reports seeking deportation on national security grounds, but only 44 people were actually removed.
This is a disaster, so will the Liberals reduce immigration levels—
The hon. Minister of Public Safety.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is a historic day for Canada. We released a national security strategy that encompasses an all-of-government approach toward strategic national security. We will, in the coming weeks and months, release specific strategies toward public safety, as well as intelligence, defence, the economy and foreign policy. This is a once-in-a-generation opportunity for us to ensure that we have a strategic view of national security.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the strategy the minister mentioned could have been an email. It was very slim, and it said nothing about one of Canada's biggest security issues, which is the failure to screen people who are coming into the country. Now the Prime Minister wants to increase immigration levels.

CSIS screening requests hit a record 538,000 in 2024, and permanent residency files for full security screening are now projected to take years to clear. Why does this national security strategy say nothing about these things?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the national security strategy is all-encompassing and has many elements of what my friend opposite is seeking. I can assure her that as part of the public safety portfolio, we are working toward finalizing a more comprehensive response that includes security screening. It is an essential part of keeping Canadians safe.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, actually, if I hit Ctrl+F on that document, I cannot find anything about improved security screening for non-citizens entering Canada. I would refer him to that document, and I would also refer him to the results. When Ahmed Eldidi entered Canada, he was allowed to do so in spite of the fact that there was a video circulating that showed him essentially committing an ISIS-level crime. He was convicted of a crime afterward, and the Persian community now wants clear public screening criteria that distinguishes forced conscripts from senior officials and terrorist leaders. Why did this strategy not do any of that?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I certainly hope the member opposite went beyond Ctrl+F to read this document. It is an essential part of ensuring the safety and security of Canadians. There are elements in there that will, over the next several weeks and months, make it abundantly clear that this is about ensuring the safety and security of every Canadian while ensuring that strategic security objectives are met.

Mr. Speaker, Liberal inflation continues to drive up the cost of living, forcing interest rates up. Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. Meanwhile, the Prime Minister's wife was just appointed as Canada's new ocean envoy, with 1.2 billion taxpayer dollars tied to these initiatives. The Liberals say that she is working for free, but unpaid should not mean unaccountable.

The minister's office will not say if she is seeking donations from banks or industry, or what government resources she is using. Conservatives tried to invite her to the fisheries and oceans committee to get answers, but the Liberals blocked it.
Why will they not allow her to come to committee?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Speaker, Canada is a world leader in oceans conservation. We have a number of programs, as the member correctly points out, to protect our oceans and protect the species, including species at risk, that exist in the oceans. We will today and tomorrow announce further measures to protect our oceans.

Many ministers are responsible for a variety of these programs. They are, of course, always accountable for the spending that is undertaken in the name of oceans conservation. We thank the Prime Minister's wife for her leadership on this file.

Mr. Speaker, having government appointees appear before committee is standard practice. The Liberals made the unusual decision to appoint the Prime Minister's wife to this role. That should mean more transparency, not less.

Lobbyists and special interest groups are celebrating that they have access to the Prime Minister's wife, and $1.2 billion is not a small amount of money. Canadians deserve to know what her responsibilities are, what authority she has and how their money is being spent.
What do the Liberals have to hide by blocking her appearance?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I just answered, the Prime Minister's spouse has volunteered to spearhead Canadian efforts in public diplomacy and oceans conservation. Ministers remain responsible and accountable for answering any and all questions about our programming on oceans conservation.
What I would like to know in terms of accountability—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The minister can continue.

Mr. Speaker, what I would like to know in terms of accountability is where the member was when we announced $70 billion of investment at Churchill Falls, which is going to put Newfoundlanders and Labradorians to work for the next generation. She was nowhere to be found. Let us have accountability, please.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals sure talk a good game. They are like the used car salesman people really like, until their tire falls off as they are driving home.

Let me explain. Every day, they get up and talk about how they are there for Canadian businesses and for workers, yet when National Steel Car got in touch seeking tariff relief, what did it get? It got crickets. It makes steel railcars with 98% Canadian content.
When it actually matters, why are the Liberals always either MIA or sending useless letters?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, useless letters? Clearly, someone here is out of touch with reality.

A letter that contains a commitment by the Government of Canada to assist a company to modernize, to buy new equipment, to expand production and to find new markets, is that a useless letter? I could have many other letters like that. That is what we have been doing over the past six months.
Mr. Speaker, I am really glad the member wants some reality. Let us have some reality.

Stellantis needed help from the government. What did it get? Nothing. CAMI needed support from the government. What did it get? Nothing. PACCAR needed support from the government. What did it get? Nothing. Algoma needed support from the government. What did it get? Nothing. Stelco workers needed support from the government. What did they get? They got a useless letter.
Now National Steel Car needs help from the government. What is it going to get, another useless letter?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Algoma Steel? Do you really want to go there?
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
It is not me who wants to go there. Members can go where they want, but I do not care.
The hon. member may continue.

Mr. Speaker, on Algoma Steel, we have been trying, and succeeding, to keep the company alive and help it pivot to a new way of making steel so that it can be the preferred supplier of high-quality steel for the shipbuilding industry.
Algoma Steel, really?

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals' abandonment of the steel sector is causing tremendous harm to Canadian workers. Following the loss of 500 jobs at Stelco, another 2,000 jobs are now being lost across Canada. In recent months, dozens of Quebec businesses have contacted us to denounce the Liberal government, which is completely out of touch with reality. These businesses have submitted concrete recommendations to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry in hopes of securing their survival.
My question is simple: Why has neither of these Liberal ministers listened to Quebec businesses?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Carlos Leitão (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have been doing exactly that for at least six months, especially in my colleague's region and in the Centre-du-Québec region. We have visited dozens of small and medium-sized businesses.

Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions has programs tailored to the tariff response to assist businesses. My colleague should speak with these businesses, because they will confirm what we have done over the past six months and will continue to do.

Mr. Speaker, first nations and Inuit policing is a matter of fairness and equity. Policing in first nations and Inuit communities has been underfunded for far too long. The courts and the Parliamentary Budget Officer have told us that clearly.

This week, the Prime Minister convened a first ministers' meeting with first nations leadership for the first time in over two decades to advocate shared priorities, including on security and community safety, and announced historic funding of close to $634 million over four years and over $250 million annually to renew and expand first nations and Inuit policing agreements.
Can the Minister of Public Safety update this House and Canadians on that?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gary Anandasangaree (Minister of Public Safety, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for Sault Ste. Marie—Algoma for his hard work and advocacy.

Every indigenous community deserves to feel and be safe. This historic funding supports police services such as the Tsuut'ina Nation Police Service in Alberta. This is on top of the $140 million for indigenous-led crime prevention and public safety programming, like community safety officers. These investments in policing support community-led solutions, close gaps and ensure that indigenous people have the tools they need to ensure their safety and security.

Mr. Speaker, the Bank of Canada's October report indicates that inflation is at nearly 3%, economic growth is less than 1%, thousands of jobs are being lost, businesses are cutting back on investment and, month after month, they are absorbing the cost of tariffs, but at some point they will have to pass them on to consumers.
On top of all that, the policy rate went up. That is the result of the Liberal strategy. Canadians are struggling to make ends meet. That is the Liberals' real record.
Will the government finally follow the Conservative plan to give Canadians some breathing room?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Caroline Desrochers (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Housing and Infrastructure, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am confused about what my colleague is saying because, quite simply, the Conservatives have no plan to make life more affordable for families.

On the contrary, they have consistently voted against everything we have done since the beginning of the year. From the very start, they have been telling us that the government has no business getting involved in building affordable housing. We are there. We are already hard at work. Rents have gone down over the past 24 months.
Tens of thousands of housing starts are under way thanks to the programs that we put in place.
Let us be serious. The Conservatives need to get to work.

Mr. Speaker, I am very proud of the plans Conservatives have announced. Just today, we announced an exciting new idea to support families: allowing both parents to simultaneously claim the CPP child-rearing dropout. This means families who share caregiving responsibilities would no longer be penalized in the calculation of their pension eligibility.
Parents should not have to choose between spending time with their kids and protecting their retirement. Will the finance minister include this constructive proposal in the upcoming budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, once again, we are going to take no lessons from the Conservatives in terms of affordability for families. We have been delivering it. We have put in place longer parental leave options, shared parental benefits, greater support for working families and, perhaps most importantly and most historically, a Canada-wide early learning and child care program saving families over $16,000 a year in some cases, which the member opposes.
Mr. Speaker, we are zero for one in terms of answering my questions.

The Bank of Canada is now confirming that it is harder than ever for unemployed Canadians to find work, as we have now hit a 29-year low in labour force participation. Meanwhile, the fisheries minister saw no problem with subsidizing a company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers.

The Liberals put the shellfish interests of this foreign company ahead of Canadian workers. Will the fisheries minister finally stand up and explain why they subsidized the company that fired Canadians to hire illegal workers?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ernie Klassen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that the Conservatives have a member from Alberta asking questions about the fisheries in Atlanta Canada.

The member is trying to spin a single project from 2024 that was not even for employment. It was for crab processing equipment. I am sure the member has no idea how the fishery works, but the Atlantic fisheries fund has funded more than 1,300 projects in communities across Atlantic Canada, and our government just signed a new deal with Atlantic provinces for $300 million in new funding.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Kristina Tesser Derksen (Milton East—Halton Hills South, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, in a shifting global economy, Canadians and businesses need fewer barriers and faster, more efficient government services. Our government recently introduced Bill S-7, the cutting red tape for all Canadians act. I would ask the President of the Treasury Board to explain how these measures will make life easier for Canadians and help Canadian businesses compete and grow.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Shafqat Ali (President of the Treasury Board, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, to grow businesses, we need to cut red tape, reduce burdens and lower costs. The cutting red tape for all Canadians act would do just that. We are focused on maintaining strong protections for public health, safety and the environment. Our goal is clear: less time on paperwork and more time to innovate.
We are building Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, farmers along the high-speed rail route want to be heard by the Liberal government, and they deserve to be heard. However, it seems that the government listens more to visitors from Europe. What is wrong with this picture? The Liberals are silencing Canadians whose land will be expropriated by European-style projects that have no guarantee of long-term profitability.
When will this Liberal government do something about Canadians' suffering by axing the federal taxes on diesel?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it should come as no surprise that the Conservatives are doubling down on their opposition to a promising project that will benefit all Quebeckers.

Of course we will continue to listen to the agricultural community when it comes to building high-speed rail. We will also continue to listen to the agricultural community when it comes to the cost of fuel. We have cut the tax and we have extended that cut in fuel prices for the farming community. We will continue to listen.

Mr. Speaker, while the Liberal government, with the help of the Conservatives, is bulldozing through the anti-environment, anti-indigenous and anti-worker Bill C-39, scientists report that fossil fuel-driven climate change caused a 275% increase in deaths due to wildfire smoke in Canada. It is proof the Liberals' corporate agenda is putting lives at risk and jeopardizing a livable planet.
Will the government listen to scientists, save lives, stop fuelling the climate emergency and withdraw Bill C-39?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Wade Grant (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Environment and Climate Change, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have to disagree. We have the best science, we have the best standards and we are going to keep to them.

I am always pleased to work with all of my colleagues here as we move forward to fight climate change and protect the environment. We have introduced the national electricity strategy, we are going to double the electrical grid by 2030, we have invested $3.8 billion in the nature strategy to protect 30% of lands and waters by 2030, and we have invested $1.2 billion to protect oceans, marine conservation, whales and indigenous partnership.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are being hammered by the rising cost of living, and yesterday brought another blow with the Bank of Canada hiking interest rates for the first time since 2023. This means higher credit card bills, bigger mortgage payments and more expensive loans for working families. It will put added strain on small businesses and things will get worse. The Bank of Canada forecasts inflation to soar through 2027.
Why is the Liberal government failing to bring down the cost of living and make life more affordable for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Ryan Turnbull (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance and National Revenue and to the Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we know that the Bank of Canada and its monetary policy are independent. It has to keep inflation within the target range. Obviously, inflation is being driven by conflicts in the Middle East and the oil price shocks. The member opposite knows that well.

We have invested in the Canadian economy. We have strengthened affordability supports and measures, and social support programs like the groceries and essentials benefit. That is real support. It amounts to thousands of dollars per month with child care, dental care and the national school food program. There are all kinds of supports that really impact families' lives. That makes life easier.
We are doing all that while investing in a more prosperous future.
I would like to draw the attention of members to the presence in the gallery of the Hon. Cory Bellmore, Minister of Community Services for the Yukon Territory.
Some hon. members: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have a point of order arising out of question period. We have just been through a difficult and divisive separation referendum in Alberta, where many of us worked hard to make the case for the equality of all provinces and the right of all provinces to be heard. That includes the right of representatives from every region in the House to be heard and to speak about national issues.
During question period, a parliamentary secretary made decidedly unparliamentary remarks, disparaging the right of members from Alberta to participate in national conversations on national issues—
It would not be proper if somebody did that, but unfortunately, the Chair did not hear that. It would not be proper for a member to say that to another member from any province.
An hon. member: Oh, oh!
The Speaker: I do not know who it was. I will check the record.

Mr. Speaker, it is always an honour for me to rise in place of the House leader for the official opposition to ask this question. As he says every time, all Canadians are eagerly awaiting this moment. This is an opportunity for us to ask the government what is in store for us next week.

However, before we look ahead to next week, it is worth taking a brief look back. It was a tough week for the government, especially when we learned from the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report that $703 billion would be added to the national debt over the next five years. We also learned that inflation is up to 3.1% and that the Bank of Canada has raised interest rates. Finally, the Governor of the Bank of Canada told us that families will unfortunately have to pay more for food next year.

Next week, the government will, in a sense, turn a Thursday into a Tuesday by tabling its budget on that day, rather than on a Tuesday, as is customary in the House. We hope the Minister of Finance will include measures in this budget to bring down the cost of living so that rents are more affordable and people can continue to pay their mortgages. I also hope the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons will announce legislative measures to ensure that Canadians can keep their jobs and save money.
I look forward to my hon. government colleague's response.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it has been a historic week here in Ottawa. It culminated in our annual meeting with our friends and cousins from the European Union, with whom we are now developing deeper ties in order to diversify our foreign trade and provide Canadians with prosperity, quality of life and new employment opportunities for future generations.

Concerning the budget, I am not sure whether my esteemed colleague will like it, because it is going to focus on affordability and Canada's competitiveness. We often see that the Conservatives are not always thrilled with Canada's success. That said, we continue to act in a spirit of collaboration and reach out to our Conservative friends.
This afternoon, we will continue the debate at second reading of Bill C-34.
Tomorrow we will call Bill C-41, the medical assistance in dying safeguards act, which was introduced earlier this week.
Monday of next week shall be an opposition day.
On Tuesday and Wednesday, we will begin debate at report stage and third reading of Bill C-31, a second act to implement certain provisions of the budget tabled in Parliament on November 4, 2025.

On Thursday, we will begin debate on Bill S-5, the connected care for Canadians act, and at 4 p.m., as my esteemed colleague mentioned, the Minister of Finance and National Revenue will deliver his budget speech.
I have the honour to lay upon the table the House of Commons Administration's strategic plan 2027–31.
I have the honour to inform the House that a communication has been received as follows:

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-34, An Act to enact the Digital Safety Act and the Digital Safety Commission of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other Acts, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: The hon. member for Sherbrooke has three minutes and 25 seconds remaining.

Mr. Speaker, I was saying that a group of students from the faculty of law at Université de Sherbrooke had drafted a bill setting the minimum age for accessing social media at 16. They drew a parallel with substances such as alcohol and tobacco. Obviously, these substances are comparable not only because they are addictive but also because of their adverse effect on health. This student-led initiative resulted in Bill 796 in Quebec City and received unanimous support when it was introduced in June 2026.

I would also like to highlight the commitment of the Sherbrooke region's school services centre, which has launched a program called “Social Media: Connected, Safe and Legal” to provide parents with resources on cybersecurity, cyber-bullying, and privacy.

This brings me to the concerns that some of my colleagues may have about this bill. Freedom of expression is a known and important concern, but it is fully integrated into the bill we are proposing. Young people under the age of 16 will still be able to express themselves online. The only difference is that they will do so on platforms that are not considered addictive and that will not put them in harm's way. The commission created under this act will also have the authority to exempt services from this minimum age requirement as long as they provide adequate child protection guarantees. My colleague, the member for Outremont, aptly said in her speech last week: “Safety must be a design choice too.”

Canadians want us to take effective action on solving this problem. We should also keep in mind that the digital platforms already apply a default condition that requires users to be at least 13 years of age. This bill would raise that condition only slightly but would produce considerable benefits.

Healthy children are the foundation of a healthy society. Honestly, I fear for the state of our society in the not-too-distant future if we fail to adapt to the forces that are disrupting it. The fact is that Canada is fully capable of responding proactively to the changes brought about by this new digital era. We have a fundamental obligation to today's young people and to future generations.

Everyone gathered here today is already aware of these issues. We know they are gaining momentum, so let us get to work. Let us ensure that our laws keep pace with society's needs. The House sees its share of disagreements, and that is healthy. Debating the issues that Canadians care about and working together to move our great country forward is part of our job description as members of Parliament. When it comes to keeping kids safe, we should all agree on one thing: We have to protect them as much as possible without infringing on their rights. That should be something we can all agree on.

Less than a month from now, on November 20, we will celebrate National Child Day, as we do every year. On this occasion, I will think of all the children, especially our own, and of our great responsibility to them.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I always appreciate the opportunity to have discussions with my seatmate. I know how important this issue is, and I appreciate that she has consulted with young people.

Bill C-34 would put in, through law, regulations that would protect children across the nation. I see that as a very strong positive. Not only would it provide the opportunity to have regulations for service providers and AI chatbots, but it would also provide the opportunity to institute fines through the establishment of a commission.
I am wondering if my friend could provide her thoughts on how important it is that we bring forward the legislation and ultimately see it pass, because it is all about protecting our children.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague, whom I hold in high regard.
The creation of this commission will help ensure that regulations are complied with and that service providers are held to account. This is another step in keeping our children safe.

Mr. Speaker, there is no question that as legislators, we should be doing everything we need to do to protect children. I do not think anybody in the House would disagree with that. There are concerns, however, which I have been hearing from my constituents and people right across the country, that under section 2(b) of the charter, the potential exists for an infringement of rights and freedoms. That is for privacy rights as well.

When this bill goes to committee, there is going to be a lot of discussion. A lot of witnesses are going to come forward and talk about that. I am wondering if the hon. member has been hearing from her constituents about some of those concerns as well.

Mr. Speaker, young people will still be allowed to use social media and other platforms. Bill C-34 will simply make the use of those platforms less harmful to children. We are protecting them by limiting their access to certain content. According to Statistics Canada, one in eight children see content that incites hatred or violence every day without even searching for it, which is why it is so important to move forward with Bill C-34.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a comment and ask a question.

The Standing Committee on the Status of Women's last two studies have addressed the issue of social media. When we looked at this issue as part of our study on the rise of masculinism and anti-feminism, witnesses told us that we needed to find a way to better legislate online behaviour, such as cyber-violence.

The committee is currently conducting a study on the disproportionate impact of AI on women. People shared their concerns with us about social media and AI, and they spoke about Bill C-34. This bill may not solve everything.
How will Bill C-34 help with rise of masculinism and anti-feminism and with the disproportionate impact of AI on women and girls?

Madam Speaker, studies and analyses do indeed show that women are disproportionately affected by everything that happens online. In fact, colleagues in the Pacific region have launched a free program called Face Forward, which was developed by Areto. This initiative protects female members of Parliament by giving them access to all kinds of resources and a network through which they can communicate. An initiative like this is important. However, everything we are proposing in Bill C-34 is also a very good solution.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak to Bill C-34 today, a bill that was first introduced back in June. Here we are, almost at the beginning of November, and we are dealing with what I believe to be a consequential piece of legislation that does not come without some concern. It will be good when this bill goes to committee, so that stakeholders, advocates of online safety and those who are concerned about civil liberties and rights can have their say. I expect that it will be a pretty long job for the committee to look at this bill to make sure that what comes back to the House reflects a balance in what should be the ultimate priority for any parliamentarian. I believe that most reasonable-thinking people in this country would agree that the protection of children online is paramount to our role as members of Parliament, as legislators, as those who make the laws.

I know that parents, because I have heard from many in my riding, are concerned about the proliferation of online activity that involves bullying, algorithm effects and content meant to draw in young people, keep them online and keep them engaged for whatever reason. Of course, one of the biggest concerns is individuals who are contacting young people under the guise of being somebody else. They are doing it in many cases to bully them or for nefarious reasons. We have a responsibility to make sure that we are protecting our children. Nobody in this House would disagree with that, but as I said, there are some concerns.

There are some principles we need to be looking at with respect to this. All of us agree that children should not be exposed to sexually explicit content online. Platforms have a responsibility to ensure that children cannot access this type of material. They should be protected from people who seek to exploit or harm them online. Children should also be protected from online content and platform features that contribute to poor mental health outcomes. That was outlined in Bill C-216, which was a private member's bill introduced by the member for Calgary Nose Hill. It was done sincerely and with the intent to protect children online from poor mental health outcomes as a result of the online content that is bombarding young people day in and day out.

I recall that recently, I was in Toronto riding on the subway heading downtown. I was on my phone, as most Canadians are, and I could see the age demographics of the people who were on that train. When we are on a subway, there is nothing better to do than look at our phones, and I saw that everyone was engaged in some sort of online activity. They would have been bombarded with algorithms. They would have been bombarded with content that was meant to keep them engaged.

Platforms should also be held accountable for the swift removal of non-consensually distributed intimate images, including those generated by AI, while taking proactive steps to prevent them from being uploaded in the first place. As colleagues know, I chair the ethics committee. We just recently concluded a study on artificial intelligence and the impact that it is going to have. It went down a dark place involving superintelligence and computers talking to computers. That report, I expect, will be tabled in this House in the next couple of weeks. There were some very significant recommendations the committee made to harness the impact that artificial intelligence is having with respect to what I said earlier: superintelligence, computers talking to computers and how that is going to impact things.

Already, we are seeing online that artificial intelligence is having a huge impact on people's lives. I get phone calls in my office from people asking me whether content online is artificial intelligence or real. My own mom has called me, asking, “Johnny, I just saw this thing on Facebook. Is it true or not?”

It is having a significant impact on overall online activity, but it is also having an impact on what the truth is. Oftentimes, we couch things as misinformation and disinformation. I have said it before and I will say it again: I am old enough to remember when misinformation and disinformation were known as lying. It is a serious problem when these algorithms pick up the content that people are looking at and then, as I said earlier, bombard them with more of this content. Oftentimes, things are not real. Online companies have a responsibility to swiftly remove, especially, the non-consensual intimate images that we have heard so many stories about, with young people's images being put online. When they are online, they are online forever. We need to make sure that we are working as legislators to protect that as well.

Ultimately, parents remain the primary decision-makers. Governments and platforms should support and not replace any parental autonomy when it comes to this stuff. Having four kids, I am often not aware, if at all, of what content they are looking at. They are adults, but it was like that even when they were younger. It seems that every child is getting phones so they can stay in contact with their family. I do not know what the minimum age is, whether it is eight, nine or 10, but what are they looking at?

Parents have an obligation, but we also have an obligation to help parents in that regard. Frankly, parents should be empowered to use the tools they need to protect their children online, whether it is with granting permission or with buttons, whatever the case is and whatever we can come up with. Bill C-34 addresses many concerns in regard to that. We should be giving parents an opportunity to deal with it.

Ultimately, as chair of the access to information, privacy and ethics committee, I know that privacy becomes paramount. We have an institution in this place that is led by the Privacy Commissioner to make sure that privacy is protected. That should be the ultimate goal of what we are trying to do. When this bill gets to committee, I am sure that privacy experts and those who are interested in the protection of privacy will testify.

Canadians have the right to express themselves freely online. Governments and platforms should not restrict lawful speech. There are two sides to this. We are talking about the protection of children, but we are also talking about the protection of the rights and liberties of parents and individuals, even in the case of political discourse, to express themselves freely online without fear of any government involvement, or law enforcement involvement in this case, especially when we are talking about freedoms online. We need to protect, as much as we can, the rights and freedoms of individuals to express themselves freely.

We need to protect children, but that should not be used as an excuse to invoke oversight on law-abiding citizens. That is the hallmark of any free and democratic society. Again, protecting children becomes paramount here.

In conclusion, I will reiterate that as Bill C-34 progresses through today and progresses through committees, it will be vitally important that we protect children online and give parents the tools they need in order to do that, but we cannot do that at the cost of our civil liberties and the rights and freedoms of individuals to express themselves in a law-abiding manner.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I appreciate many of the comments the member put on the record.

I too am very much concerned about things like algorithms. I am very much concerned about the harmful content out there today. That is why Bill C-34 would establish a framework that would see regulations put in place to protect the children of Canada. That is a significant thing. Not only would it put in place regulations or allow for them, but it would also put in place a commission. Through that commission, we could see fines. The bottom line is that there would be more accountability on things like service providers, platforms, AI chatbots and so forth.
Does the member agree with the principle of having a commission to ensure that we see follow-up, a commission that has a high level of expertise on the issue?

Madam Speaker, I think I made it very clear, in the 10 minutes I had, how important it is to protect our children. We also have to make sure that we are not doing that at a cost to civil liberties and rights, especially for law-abiding people, to express themselves online. We have to find that balance. Bill C-34 has a lot more work to do. It will go to committee. We will hear from experts. We will hear from witnesses who are concerned about both sides of the issue. We will certainly hear from child advocates. Of course, we support that.

The other thing is that it is a rapidly changing environment with artificial intelligence, chatbots and everything. My biggest fear is that this legislation will not keep up enough for the changes that are coming. This is certainly something we heard at the ethics committee. We heard how rapidly artificial intelligence is occurring, and we are going to have to be nimble to make sure that we make the changes that are necessary in this rapidly evolving environment of artificial intelligence online.

Madam Speaker, the bill would defer many important details by delegating responsibility for these matters to the commission it seeks to create, the digital safety commission of Canada, a new federal bureaucracy. A number of contentious issues remain unaddressed in the bill, which seems to set out broad principles, delegating the details to the commission for later consideration.

Does my colleague agree that all potentially contentious issues should be addressed and studied as fully as possible so that the law reflects the legislative intent and so that responsibility is not unduly delegated to officials?

Madam Speaker, I agree with the hon. member. There are many aspects of the bill that concern me, such as the point the hon. member raised. That is why it is very important that, when the bill goes to committee, we have a thorough discussion on everything it contains. Protecting children is very important, but protecting the rights and freedoms of individuals in Canada is what worries me and many other people. We need to discuss that soon.
Madam Speaker, there are many parents who have reached out to a number of MPs. They are very concerned about their ability to protect their children, and they are asking for additional assistance.

Does the member believe that there is a way to balance the rights of individual freedoms so that people are not unfairly targeted for lawful conduct online while parents can be given the tools to protect their children without government intervention?

Madam Speaker, that is the fine balance we have to find. It is about protecting children, which we all want, and then protecting law-abiding people who are expressing their views from a knock on the door by the police telling them they have expressed themselves too much—
I beg members not to use actions such as knocking on the table. It is very disturbing for the interpreters.
Resuming debate, the hon. member for Mississauga—Malton.
Madam Speaker, freedom of speech has its place. Let me say that first, because it is where this debate must begin, and nothing in this bill changes it.
The question before us is a different one. How do we use a technology without building a society that is splintered by thought?

We have a society of isolated groups that are increasingly speaking past one another, whose ideas are reinforced whether they are the brightest glimmers of hope that come with the dawn of a new generation or the darkest of thoughts only shared behind a screen through a fictional ID and the clicks of a keyboard. I speak, of course, of social media, and we should make no mistakes about its dangers. Biases are being reinforced. Isolation is increasing. In the space that exists between us, there are those who insert misinformation on purpose.

Social media was meant to be a common space, a space that was created to bring people together, but its very essence is more divisive than it has ever been. Its guardrails are intentionally taken down, and it is increasingly a place of bots and misinformation intentionally injected to create division and chaos. That matters more than ever, because these platforms have become for many Canadians a source of news and information.

I am old enough to remember that, when I was growing up, there was a set number of channels we watched and, in my father's generation, a set of radio stations he would listen to on his morning drives. We were given, within reasonable bounds, a common set of facts we could all agree upon, a shared reality. Today, we live in a world where inconvenient facts can be spun as lies and expedient conjecture can pass for truth. The information we get from search and social media is subject to manipulation and uneven distortions.

When social media was in its early days, there was a great hope that it would become the new public square, a space where people could come together and discuss things freely without fear of retribution or censorship, but what we have seen, when these companies engage in content moderation, or worse distortion, and individuals hide behind fictional identities, is that social media has become less of a public square and more of a space of silos, where hatred is monetized, with little room left for robust public debate. If we, as relatively informed adults, have become so susceptible to lies and conspiracy theories from social media, we should be concerned about the effects on those whose minds are still developing.

Social media companies engage in content moderation. The problem is that the industry standards have fallen. Children are entering the digital world at ever younger ages, often without their parents' knowledge. With a few clicks, a child can open an account on a platform designed to hold their attention, expose them to harm and collect their personal data. The evidence is serious. Youth who experience online victimization report three times the suicide ideation. Over the past decade, depression among Canadians 15 to 24 has doubled, and anxiety has quadrupled. In 2023 alone, police recorded almost 20,000 incidents of online child sexual exploitation. That is a 59% increase in a single year, and a 500% increase since 2014. We can tell parents to monitor more closely, but they are already stretched thin, and no one can watch a child's screen 24 hours a day. No parent can inspect an algorithm.

Here is the heart of the matter. We have laws for when the harm has already happened, but almost nothing that requires platforms to prevent it. If we have learned anything over these last years, it is that we must lower our expectations of what social media companies would do on their own and raise expectations of what government must do in their place. Government regulation must become part of the solution.

Let me say plainly what Bill C-34 does. It creates three duties: a duty to act responsibly, to assess the risks on their own platforms and reduce them by design; a duty to protect children and build age-appropriate safeguards into the product itself; and a duty to make certain content inaccessible, which requires the rapid removal of child sexual exploitation material and intimate images shared without consent, including deepfakes.

The bill would prohibit children under 16 from holding social media accounts. However, it is not a wall without a door. A platform can apply to the new digital safety commission for an exemption if it can demonstrate that its products are safe for children. The ban would give companies a reason to compete on safety, because safety is what opens the door.

AI chatbots would not face an age ban, because they would be bound by the duty to act responsibly and the duty to protect children, and they would need to direct users to intervention services when someone expresses thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Platforms would publish a digital safety plan telling Canadians what risks exist, what they are doing about them and how much harmful content has been flagged. An independent commission of three to five experts would review those plans, assess whether age verification actually works and issue penalties of up to 3% of global revenue for failure. This is lower than Australia, the EU and the U.K.

Let me address the concerns that have been raised, because they deserve a serious answer. Some will say that this would threaten free speech. I take that seriously, which is why I began where I did. Let us look at what this bill would define as harmful: content that sexually victimizes a child; intimate images shared without consent; content that induces a child into self-harm; content used to bully a child; and content that foments extreme hatred, incites violence, or promotes terrorism. These categories are narrow and clearly defined.

This bill would not touch everyday conversation or lawful debate. The commission would have no power to arrest anyone. The bill would place responsibility on the platforms, not on citizens. Some will say this bill invades privacy, but private messaging would be specifically exempt. Data gathered for age verification would be securely collected and swiftly destroyed. The bill would not dictate one method. It would put the onus on platforms to build systems and on the independent commission to judge whether they are adequate.

Others will say this is simply another layer of bureaucracy. I would ask them what the alternative is. Is it leaving it to the companies we have just discussed, or to politicians trading shots across this chamber every time a crisis breaks? The purpose of an expert, independent commission is to take this issue out of political point scoring and replace it with consistent, measured expertise. There are critics who say the commission's details remain unclear. I think that is a fair point. Some respected scholars have called it opaque, and some groups are withholding full support until the regulations are final, but the commission must be independent, and prescribing every decision in statute would undermine that independence.

We are acting quickly, but we intend to get this right. We are not alone. Pediatric hospitals and children's health groups have called this an important step forward. The Canadian Centre for Child Protection has called it “a crucial step”. Some, like the Phone-Free School Movement, want us to go further. This tells me that the direction is right and that the debate is about how far to go. Canadians are with us, as 77% say we should consider restricting social media for those under 16. That is true of 67% of those aged 18 to 34 and 83% of those 55 and over. It is rare to find a consensus that crosses every generation.

The question is not whether we believe in free expression; we do. The question is whether a space built for connection can once again be worthy of that name, whether our children can grow up with a shared reality, with room for real debate and with protection from those who profit from their harm. We cannot rebuild that common ground in a single bill, but we can lay the foundation for a safer space.
Let us do it. Let us pass Bill C-34.

Madam Speaker, I just want to get a couple things on the record. I actually surveyed my constituents, and the numbers the member quoted are relatively in line. Just over 60% of constituents in my riding support an age limit being put on children with access to social media, and just over 70% feel that the Government of Canada does need to do more to regulate this space.

I have two questions, though. In Bill C-34, there is no mention of the role of the parent, nor how it would enable them to help protect their children. My colleague, the member for Calgary Nose Hill, has tabled a bill, Bill C-216, that has some good clauses. When Bill C-34 bill gets to committee, does the member think there is something that could be added to it to help give parents more tools?

On the second aspect, the member talked about the expert commission, and I do not disagree with his assertion, but I wonder if he could tell us what the accountability mechanism is for those experts so that they are not buried within the bureaucracy, because, like any human being, nobody is perfect. I am a big believer in government accountability when it comes to laws that impact Canadians right across the spectrum.
Madam Speaker, I appreciate the member's comments. I really enjoy working with him at committee as well.

As to his questions, I think parenting should be left up to parents. We know that parents have tried, for the last decade-plus, to regulate the social media usage of their children, but we are still seeing problematic behaviours arise. We are still seeing problematic data that shows us that children are struggling with social media use and parents are struggling to regulate their social media use. This bill is meant to bring in government regulation where parents really are being stretched thin.

The second part of the question was in regard to the experts on the commission. I look forward to this being fleshed out in more detail. I am sure that, for the three- to five-member commission, there will be a process in place to pick the best qualified individuals to serve.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the member about his thoughts around freedom of expression and some of the criticisms that may have been expressed in this chamber regarding the bill.

Madam Speaker, freedom of speech is a concept that is fundamentally important to me as a lawyer and as a new member of the Ontario Bar. This bill does not regulate free speech. Free speech is fundamentally protected under our charter.

It does define harmful speech, and I mentioned that in my speech. These categories are narrowly defined and very clearly stated. If there is open, robust debate, that is not something that this bill is targeting.

Madam Speaker, I have a question. The Bloc Québécois wants this bill to go to committee so we can take a closer look at the commission that the government proposes to establish under this bill. This commission would be responsible for reviewing cases. However, the powers that would be granted to it appear to be quite extensive. It would be able to conduct inspections, summon witnesses and impose administrative penalties. In effect, the government is proposing to pass legislation that sets out principles while delegating all the powers to an administrative body to resolve the most contentious issues.
It is trying to keep the details away from parliamentarians. What real impact will we be able to have in relation to this commission?

Madam Speaker, I think an independent commission is necessary because, as we can see, sometimes with the debate in this chamber, it can get highly politicized. Rather than moving from crisis to crisis, the independent commission could bring measured expertise.

Canadians elected the government on a mandate to protect Canadians, especially young Canadians, whose minds are still developing. I look forward to the work that the commission will eventually do in furthering that work.

Madam Speaker, my colleague talked about a sharp rise in anxiety and depression in children. Can he tell the House what he thinks is the major cause of this crisis and what we need to do to identify the causes and potential ways to reverse this crisis?

Madam Speaker, I think the problem really arises because online spaces have become spaces of silos, where whatever beliefs or fears one has get reinforced by the algorithms. One of the ways that we can protect against that is to have an online space but then to come to a real space where we can actually have dialogue and debate.
I look forward to the work that the commission will do to help alleviate problems with the online spaces.
